title: Robinson Crusoe
alternative_titles: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, of York, Mariner
description: A first-person narrative of a mariner cast away for twenty-eight years on an uninhabited island near the mouth of the Orinoco, presented as a true history and a penitential life. It joins an extremely detailed account of material survival - building, planting, pottery, calendaring - to a providential reading of the narrator's own sins and mercies. Published in April 1719 and struck off in several issues that year, it made the individual survivor narrative the central plot of English prose fiction.
plot_or_argument: Against his father's counsel of a middle station the York mariner sails, is taken by Sale pirates, escapes, plants a plantation in Brazil, and is wrecked in a course that leaves him sole survivor on a shore. He salvages the ship, builds a fence and a country house, learns by trial and error to make boards, earthenware, bread and goats' milk, keeps a journal, and reads scripture, gradually interpreting his preservation as conversion. He discovers a footprint, then cannibal feasts, saves a captive whom he names Friday, and with Friday and a Spaniard fights off further visitors. An English ship arriving after a mutiny carries him home by way of Brazil and land travel through hostile country, and the closing narrative reports his plantation wealth and a second, briefly summarised marriage.
narrative_structure: Continuous first-person retrospect, with embedded journal entries at the centre and a list-and-inventory mode of description; the frame of an edited 'original' account allows the narrator to comment on his own earlier blindness.
principal_characters: Robinson Crusoe; Friday; Xury; the Portuguese captain of the Lisbon trade; the captain of the Brazil plantation; the mutineer mate; the Spaniard
literary_form: novel; prose fiction in the form of a spiritual autobiography and travel relation
meter_and_prosody: Unornamented prose of the low or business style, with periodic sentences, accounting clauses, inventories and repeated temporal markers ('first', 'then', 'about'); the rhythm is documentary rather than rhetorical, and the couple of passages of elevated meditation are marked off by scriptural quotation.
historical_context: Written in the spring and summer of 1719 out of real and romanced sources, including the marooned Alexander Selkirk, Spanish-American trade geography and the project-mongering literature of the 1690s, and printed in the same decade as the expansion of the plantation and slave trades. Its title-page assertion that the narrator is the author answered the contemporary vogue for detected 'memoirs'.
literary_significance: It established the material-realist individual narrative as the governing model of the rising English novel, and its treatment of labour, property, dominion and providence has made it the founding text for debates about middle-class identity, colonial possession and the philosophy of the isolated mind.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work was published without the writer's name, and the two continuations, advertised as by the same hand, establish continuity of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First issued in London in octavo on 25 April 1719 in a single volume of some 300 pages, with a second edition the following month; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition's spelling, and the Crusoe sequence is here recorded as three separate works.

title: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
alternative_titles: The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Second Part of the Life of Robinson Crusoe
description: The second of the three Robinson Crusoe volumes, issued in August 1719 after a spurious continuation had appeared in London. It returns the narrator to the island, then carries him through the East Indies, the Cape and across the deserts of Central Asia in a series of voyages that replace settlement with motion.
plot_or_argument: Crusoe revisits his island, now peopled by the mutineers he left there and by newly arrived Englishmen and Spaniards, and settles disputes over worship and government before sailing on. He is attacked off Madagascar, trades and travels through the Malay coast, China and Persia, and after a near-fatal crossing of the Great Tartary desert reaches Moscow and travels overland to England, where he finds himself unexpectedly wealthy. The volume closes with a third voyage contemplated rather than narrated.
narrative_structure: First-person retrospect in an episodic voyage sequence, the island episode framing a picaresque chain of traverses and encounters; less concentrated than the first volume and more dependent on reported incident.
principal_characters: Robinson Crusoe; the island governor; Friday's brother; the Portuguese pilot; the Tartar and Muscovite guides
literary_form: novel; prose voyage narrative with an inherited fictional persona
meter_and_prosody: Plainer and more hurried prose than the first volume, dominated by dates, distances and commoditues of trade; the meditative periodic sentence gives way to the listed itinerary.
historical_context: Composed within months of the first volume's success, it draws on East India Company and privateering narratives and expressly supersedes the pirating Continuation of the World of Robinson Crusoe published in London in mid-1719.
literary_significance: It fixed the model of the sequel and the return-novel, and its colony-building episode has been much discussed as a fable of plantation government, toleration and colonial ownership.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was advertised as the true second part to displace the anonymously pirated continuation.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in octavo, 20 August 1719, as the second volume of the Crusoe history, with a concluding advertisement for the third; modern editions usually reprint the first edition.

title: Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
alternative_titles: Serious Reflections During the Life and Afflicting Circumstances of Robinson Crusoe
description: The third Crusoe volume, a collection of meditations, dialogues and practical essays put into the mouth of the retired islander. It abandons narrative for moral reflection on providence, solitude, the fear of man, temperance and the duties of a master, and is organised as a set of numbered serious thoughts.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, now settled and prospering, meditates on the religious meanings of his preservation, debates with imagined interlocutors the questions of conscience and enthusiasm, reflects on the condition of servants, wives and children, and argues that a Christian's true business is the government of his own passions. The volume adds visionary and allegorical papers on the invisible world, including a dialogue with the soul and a description of the world of spirits.
narrative_structure: A serial of short reflective papers rather than a continuous plot, with inset dialogues and a few narrative fragments; the Crusoe persona functions as a mask for a moralist.
principal_characters: Robinson Crusoe; the imagined interlocutor; Friday as a figure of natural religion; the narrator's own soul
literary_form: meditative and didactic prose essays in a fictional persona
meter_and_prosody: Serious plain prose of the conduct-book manner, with balancing clauses, scriptural tags and the interrogative turn of meditation; the allegorical papers admit a more ornate visionary rhetoric.
historical_context: Published in the same year as the second volume and in the wake of controversies over enthusiasm and natural religion, it draws on the Puritan tradition of the serious meditation and on the 1710s vogue for soliloquy on the passions.
literary_significance: It supplies the strongest internal evidence of the moral and religious frame that contemporaries read in the first volume, and its mixed reception marked the boundary between fiction and edification in the early-eighteenth-century book trade.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested, though the volume has conventionally been treated as the weakest of the three; the title-page carries the same fictional persona as its warrant.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1720 in octavo with concurrence of the earlier volumes, and frequently omitted from nineteenth- and twentieth-century selections until scholarly reprint.

title: Moll Flanders
alternative_titles: The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders
The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders, Who Was Born in Newgate
description: The confessions of a woman born in Newgate and traded through a lifetime of marriages, thefts, transportation and, at the end, repentance. It is the century's most sustained novel of the marriage market seen as an economy, in which the heroine's calculations of fortune and status are rendered with an unashamed precision.
plot_or_argument: Raised from a gypsy boarding to a servant's place, Moll contracts successively to a brother-in-law, to a landlord, to a brewer, to a banker and to a jelly husband, each match measured in money and each ending in loss. She takes to theft in Bristol and London, is captured, tried and transported to Virginia, and there marries a planter, discovering only afterwards that the marriage was incestuous. She returns enriched, and the narrative closes with a professed reformation and a prospect of an estate.
narrative_structure: First-person confessional retrospect with a preface commending the work to readers; chronology is continuous and picaresque but tied to a recurring economic arithmetic and to a late moral frame.
principal_characters: Moll Flanders; her Newgate mother; the Lancashire landlord; the banker husband; the jelly husband; the Virginia planter husband; the Newgate gaoler
literary_form: novel; picaresque and confessional prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: Businesslike first-person prose in which figures, dates and inventories carry the moral weight; the repentance passages adopt the cadences of the penitential tract, and the irony depends on the gap between the two registers.
historical_context: Appeared in the same season as printed Newgate calendars and criminal life series, and in the decade of the 1718 Transportation Act, which made the American plantations the destination of the convicted; its marriage plots assume the property anxieties of a credit economy.
literary_significance: It is the central text for the study of early-eighteenth-century ideas of marriage, money and female dependency, and its moral ambivalence - a heroine whose virtue is her prudence - marked the distance between the amatory novel and the later novel of conduct.
attribution_notes: Attribution rests on the writer's own later acknowledgment of the work and on stylistic and bibliographical continuity with the other volumes of 1722; no contemporary external evidence survives, and the fiction of an edited memoir is retained in the preface.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1722 in one volume in octavo, with a preface on the design of the work; enlarged issues followed in the 1720s and the title was reissued in the Newgate Calendar calendar of lives.

title: A Journal of the Plague Year
alternative_titles: The Journal of the Plague Year
A Journal of the Plague Year: Being Observations or Memorials, of the Most Remarkable Occurrences
description: A week-by-week history of the London visitation of 1665, compiled as a journal by a surviving citizen and published in 1722. It is neither a memoir nor an invention but a deliberately documentary fiction, assembled from bills of mortality, medical broadsides and the city's own alarm.
plot_or_argument: H.F., a stay-and-watch baker, follows the sickness from its first appearance in parishes north of the river through the closing of houses, the weekly bills, the heaps of dead, the flight of the court and the greed of doctors and officers. He reports the Aldgate burying-ground, the mad people, the poor, and the French church; he records his own narrow escapes, his visit to a doctor's house, and the disorder of the streets. The journal ends as the mortality falls with the cold weather and the city recovers.
narrative_structure: A dated and partly weekly serial journal, impersonal and statistical in the outer parts and anxiously first-person in the visits and wanderings; the observing 'I' stands inside an impersonal civic record.
principal_characters: H.F. the baker; his brother the physician; the watchmen, searchers and buryers of the parishes; the doctors and the mountebanks
literary_form: documentary and pseudo-journalistic prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: Austere prose of numeration and specification, with bills, tables and parish totals quoted as authority; the rhetorical heightening is confined to the passages of remonstrance with the city's wickedness.
historical_context: Written nearly sixty years after the event during a period of continental plague scares, and built on the bills of mortality, visitation archives and printed accounts of 1665; its publication coincided with a wider antiquarian revival of interest in the city's catastrophe.
literary_significance: It is the model of empirical urban narrative in English fiction and a foundational text for the history of the epidemic as a literary form, its mixture of statistic and fear defining how the disaster city is later fictionalised.
attribution_notes: The text was inscribed with the initials 'H.F.' and long read as a genuine memoir; attribution to the author of the 1719-22 fiction is now generally accepted on stylistic and bibliographical grounds and is here recorded as single authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1722 in octavo; a manuscript version, differing in detail, circulated in the eighteenth century and was printed in the nineteenth, and the standard text follows the first printed edition.

title: Colonel Jack
alternative_titles: The Life and Unexpected Fortunes of Jack the Thoughtful
The Fortunes and Misfortunes of Jack the Thoughtful
description: The life of a boy taken from a Newgate-connected childhood into a career of theft, transportation, soldiering and finally plantation ownership. It is the third and most openly autobiographical of the 1722 criminal narratives, with a narrator whose self-examination is obsessive and whose social climbing is a study in the making of a gentleman.
plot_or_argument: Jack, the son of a widowed mother left in want, is apprenticed to a dancing master, runs away to London, and is drawn into a gang of child thieves drilled by an old pickpocket. He is tried and transported, escapes in America, and after a series of raids and duels becomes a planter; he raises horse in the wars in Flanders, takes the title in the army, and returns to England to marry. Throughout, the narrative pauses to audit his own motives and to count his shifts from honour to criminality and back.
narrative_structure: First-person autobiography in two parts closing in a conversion narrative, moving from picaresque episode to moral accounting; the narrator repeatedly interrupts himself to examine his own designs.
principal_characters: Colonel Jack; his mother and sister; the dancing master; the old pickpocket and the child gang; the Virginia and Carolina landlords; his several wives
literary_form: novel; picaresque autobiography in prose
meter_and_prosody: Colloquial, garrulous first-person prose heavy with cant terms of the flash languages and with the accounting idiom of estates; the repentance sections adopt the periodic syntax of the serious address.
historical_context: Published in the same current of Newgate biography as the criminal lives of 1722, and drawing on the post-1718 transportation trade and on the war in the Low Countries, which supplies the military career of the title.
literary_significance: It is the most candid analysis in early fiction of class mobility and of the moral vocabulary of repentance as a social credential, and its child-thief episodes are a primary source for the history of London street life.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested in modern scholarship; the first part's title-page attributes the work to the author of Moll Flanders.
bibliographical_notes: Part I appeared in London in 1722 and Part II in 1723, both in octavo; the two parts were early bound together, and nineteenth-century reprints occasionally abridge the cant.

title: Roxana
alternative_titles: The Fortunate Mistress: Or, a History of the Life and Most Surprising Adventures of a Lady
description: The last and most searching of the great fictional confessions of the 1720s, the career of a woman who converts her own person into an asset and rises from a silk-stockinger's daughter to the mistress of a duke and the envy of the town. It is the most coolly ironic of the series, withholding the penitence its heroine repeatedly promises and making the reader wait for an ending the narrative refuses to supply.
plot_or_argument: Married against her inclination and then abandoned by a husband ruined in trade, she persuades herself that virtue is a word used by the poor to keep them poor, and becomes successively the wife, mistress and pensioner of a series of men in England and on the Continent, accumulating fortunes in Holland and Paris. She returns to London, is courted by a nobleman whom she refuses to marry, discovers that a former husband and her own daughter have tracked her down, and ends in want and remorse, the loss of her child and the collapse of her design being the catastrophe she cannot argument her way out of.
narrative_structure: First-person confessional retrospect with a self-consciously unfinished close; the irony is generated by the gap between the narrator's casuistry and the events she reports, and the Dutch and French sections slow into a series of reckonings.
principal_characters: Roxana; her husband the silk merchant; the Scottish landowner; the Duke of M.; the Dutch merchant; Susan, the lost daughter; Amy, the confidante
literary_form: novel; confessional and picaresque prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: An elaborate argumentative prose of casuistry, full of self-interrogation, exclamation and the repeated counting of stocks; the colloquy with Amy supplies a dialogue of conscience inside the monologue.
historical_context: Published in 1724 in the wake of the South Sea bubble and its aftermath of fortune-hunters and bigamy scandals, and drawing on the continental travel and money-market knowledge of the author's earlier project writing.
literary_significance: It is the most radical study of the marriage market in early fiction and a key text for the debate about whether the eighteenth-century novel could represent female desire without punishing it; its unfinished ending has generated a large critical literature.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the name Roxana is the heroine's own assumption in the narrative and the convenient title established by later editors.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1724 in one volume in octavo; reprinted in the Newgate-derived collections of lives, and modern standard editions follow the first edition.

title: The Political History of the Devil
alternative_titles: The Political History of the Devil, as the Present Governor of the World
description: A satirical history of the world written as the biography of the Devil, shown as the true political manager of modern Europe. Its argument is that the powers, churches, courts and trading companies of the world are all in leaguement with the old serpent, and that political Christianity is a mask for interest.
plot_or_argument: The Devil organises the governments of Europe by the machinery of interest, war and party; he plants the church at Rome, presides at the courts of princes, funds the stock-jobbers, and sets the faction of the enthusiasts against the settled clergy. A narrative of his own history, from his first settlement in Britain to the present, is interrupted by political dissertations and by the ironic apologies of the editor. The closing papers judge the nation's management by the standard of diabolical policy and find it creditable.
narrative_structure: A mock-history in two main books combining chronicle, dialogue and dissertation, with a heavily ironic prefatorial apparatus; a second part issued some years later repeats the design with more explicit party reference.
principal_characters: the Devil; his cabinet council; the European princes and politicians as his correspondents; the editor-narrator
literary_form: political satire in mock-historical prose
meter_and_prosody: Deadpan ironic prose of the historical narrative, with the flat connectives of chronicle used to hold absurd conclusions together; the prefaces heighten the register for satiric effect.
historical_context: Published in 1720 during the South Sea explosion and the quarrel over the ministry, in the same season as the author's other diabolical and project histories, and in the tradition of the Devil as political narrator running back to the seventeenth-century diabolica politia.
literary_significance: It is the most sustained of the early-eighteenth-century satires that read modern politics as providential machinery inverted, and a central text for the study of the Devil as a figure for commercial and political modernity.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume appeared with the same prefatorial persona as the other political histories of the period, and its party allusions are consistent with the author's known positions.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1720 in octavo; a second part followed in 1725, and the whole was reprinted in the collected political and commercial works.

title: The Consolidator
alternative_titles: The Consolidator: Or, A Dream of the Court of Great Britain
description: A political dream vision in which the narrator is carried to a moon court and given a flying machine, the Consolidator, with which he surveys the British parliament, church and party system. It is the earliest of the great Augustan satiric fictions and a direct attack on the ministry of the day and on the traffic in addresses and votes.
plot_or_argument: Summoned before the emperor of the moon, the narrator receives the Consolidator and a commission to report on the state of Great Britain. He flies over London, watches the Commons sit, and sees the ministers voting Purgatory, the sale of boroughs and the address-makers at work. He is present at the trial of the party leaders before the moon court, where the factions plead their causes, and the dream ends with a sentence upon the nation's corrupt management.
narrative_structure: A first-person dream vision in the classical manner, framing a series of satirical tableaux and set-piece orations; the moon book supplies the apparatus, the London book the invective, and the trial the formal conclusion.
principal_characters: the narrator-dreamer; the emperor of the moon; the Consolidator machine personified; the party leaders at the bar; the address-makers and the voting politicians
literary_form: political satire; prose dream vision and mock-utopian travel
meter_and_prosody: Spare ironic prose alternating with formally declaimed speeches and inserted verse addresses; the invective passages rise into the periods of pulpit and stage rhetoric for satiric effect.
historical_context: Published in 1705 in the heat of the Junto ministry crisis and the debate over the Scottish union, and dedicated into the interest of the Godolphin-Marlborough administration; its imagery draws directly on the party pamphlet war of the season.
literary_significance: It anticipates the machinery of the later Augustan dream satire and stands with the moon-project pamphlets as the founding text of the fiction of political flight; it also evidences the early use of the miscellany press for party work.
attribution_notes: Attribution established by internal and bibliographical evidence and accepted without serious dispute; the first issue was printed without the writer's name.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1705 in octavo with the descriptive title-page enumeration of the dream's parts; reissued in the same year and collected in the later political works.

title: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
alternative_titles: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters: Or, Proposals for the Establishment of the Church
description: A pamphlet written in the voice of a high-flown Church extremist, proposing that the only safe way with the Dissenters is to repeat the severity of the Counter-Reformation and destroy them root and branch. Its ironical impersonation was widely missed, and its writer was pursued for it some years later.
plot_or_argument: A mock-moderate opening complains that the Church has been tamely forbearing, then argues that the sectaries are the real enemies of the constitution and of the settled clergy. It draws the analogy with popery, demands the closing of the meeting-places and the disabling of dissenters from trade and office, and concludes that if the laws will not do the work the people must burn them out. The appended defence explains the design as satire against the extremists of both sides.
narrative_structure: A short impersonative polemic in a single sustained voice, with a self-explaining apparatus of preface and defence attached at the later issues.
principal_characters: the impersonated High Church projector; the dissenting minister; the addressers and the zealots of the Church; the legislator addressed by the pamphlet
literary_form: ironical political pamphlet; persona satire
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the impassioned party harangue, mimicking the cadences and scriptural tags of the extremist pulpit; the irony is carried by an overwrought syntax of peroration.
historical_context: Issued in February 1697/8 in the debate over the standing army, the Triennial Act and the toleration settlement; the writer was arrested in 1703 after a renewed issue, tried for a notorious libel and put in the pillory, an event made memorable in the verse of the day. Recorded here in this installment because it anchors an Augustan career, its date falling on the boundary of the period.
literary_significance: It is the classical instance of impersonative satire failing and succeeding simultaneously, the mask worn so exactly that it provoked the prosecution it was designed to discredit, and a case study in the law of seditious libel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the author both acknowledged and defended the design in the follow-up pamphlets, and the prosecution of 1703 establishes responsibility.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1697/8 as a short pamphlet of a few sheets, with issues in 1702-3 bearing the added defence; the year is given here in the Old Style dating conventionally cited for the first issue.

title: A General History of the Pyrates
alternative_titles: A General History of the Pyrates, From Their First Rise and Settlement in the Island of Providence
description: The chief narrative source for the lives of the great pirates of the American station, compiled and dramatised as a history of the profligate colony of the Bahamas. Its first volume is a continuous series of captains' lives, and its style is a hybrid of the criminal biography, the sea narrative and the moralising tale.
plot_or_argument: The work traces the rise of pyrating after the peace discharged the privateers, describes the settlement at New Providence under Hornigold and the seizures made by the new confederacy, and then gives the careers, customs, articles, trials and deaths of the principal captains. It dwells on Roberts's articles and discipline, on the terrors of Teach, and on the female pirates' disguise and capture. It moralises throughout on the inevitable end of the pyrating course, so that even the successful captains are reported into the gallows or the desert.
narrative_structure: A serial of biographical lives inside a short historical introduction, with inserted documents such as articles and trial reports; a second volume extends the series with a more evidently inventive manner.
principal_characters: Henry Every; Blackbeard; Bartholomew Roberts; Henry Jennings; Charles Vane; Anne Bonny; Mary Read
literary_form: collective biography and historical narrative in prose
meter_and_prosody: Plain narrative prose of the criminal life, with sea-cant, trial reportage and the abrupt sentences of the hanging report; the inserted documents preserve official and notarial styles.
historical_context: Published in London between 1724 and 1728 in the wave of public interest following the vice-admiralty trials of the pirates, and drawing on the court records, the colonial news sheets and the captains' own depositions.
literary_significance: It is the sourcebook of the modern image of piracy, the black flag, the articles and the ship's democracy, and one of the most influential of the Newgate-derived prose series; its uncertain authorship makes it a test case for the attribution of hack history.
attribution_notes: Attribution disputed: the first volume was entered in the name of Captain Charles Johnson, a pseudonym many scholars have identified with the novelist and pamphleteer of the same publishing circle, while others deny the identification and question the second volume; the record is held for that disputed ascription and the pseudonym alone is named in the text.
bibliographical_notes: Volume I printed in London in 1724 in octavo, with a second edition in the same year and Volume II in 1728; the standard scholarly reading text follows the third edition with collation of the differing issues.

title: The New Atalantis
alternative_titles: The New Atalantis: A Romance. Designed for a Secret History of the Present Juncto
description: A political romance and secret history of the Whig Junto, published in August 1709 and prosecuted for libel in the following November. Under the disguise of an Italianate island court it reports the sexual and fiscal intrigues of the ministers, turning the key of romantic fiction into an instrument of party attack.
plot_or_argument: A company of ladies and gallants recounting the histories of the great are led by the goddess Intrepida through the courts and closets of Atalantis. There they see the ministers intrigue for money and for the persons of their female dependants: the snares laid for the yielding, the bribery of the chamber, the ruin of the too frank and the triumph of the crafty. The tales end in exposure and desertion, and the framing discourse claims that Atalantis is a transparent name for England, so that the reader is invited to apply the key herself.
narrative_structure: An embedded-tale romance with a framing dialogue, in which reported histories of seduction are stitched together by allegorical presentation; the key is offered openly in the argument and the prefatorial matter.
principal_characters: Intrepida; Delia; Countess de Verruyse; the Duke of Sidonia; the gallants and the betrayed women of the Atalantis court
literary_form: political romance and secret history in prose
meter_and_prosody: The high romantic prose style of the amatory fiction, with elaborate periods, apostrophe and euphemistic detail of the bed-chamber, used to carry identifiable party scandal.
historical_context: Published in the last years of the Godolphin ministry and reprinted several times before the Sacheverell season; its libel prosecution in November 1709 was pressed and then dropped with the change of administration, an event central to the history of the press.
literary_significance: It is the most successful of the early key-writing romances and the text that showed how the amatory plot could be turned to party work; it shaped the later secret history and the scandalous novel of the 1720s.
attribution_notes: Attribution established by the contemporary party attacks and by the author's own defence of the design; the first issue was published without the writer's name.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1709 in two volumes in octavo, with several issues and a later continuation; discussion standardly follows the first edition with the added argument of the second issue.

title: The Adventures of Rivella
alternative_titles: The Adventures of Rivella: Or, The History of the Author of the New Atalantis. Written, By HERSELF
description: An autobiographical romance in which the author of the political secret history appears disguised as Rivella and tells the story of her own literary and amorous career. It is one of the earliest English examples of a writer using fiction to account for her own publication, her prosecution and her reputation.
plot_or_argument: Rivella, a young woman of parts and no fortune, is pressed by need and by the examples of the writers about her into authorship; she composes verses, romances and a political key-history, and moves through a society of courtiers, book publishers and rival wits. She tells how her performances brought her fame, malice and a prosecution, and how she answered her enemies by writing again. The narrative closes with her retired from the town, reflecting on the price paid by a woman who publishes.
narrative_structure: First-person fictional autobiography addressed to a companion of letters, framed as a paper written by herself; episodes of career and courtship alternate with reflections on the conditions of authorship.
principal_characters: Rivella; her mother and patroness; the book-publishers and duellers of the town; the rival wit of the playhouse quarrel; the companion to whom the paper is addressed
literary_form: fictional autobiography and confession in prose
meter_and_prosody: Conversational prose of the familiar romantic style, light, ironic and unapologetic, with inserted verses and letter-forms.
historical_context: Published in 1714 in the season of the author's last quarrels and the fall of her party, and attached to a volume reissuing her earlier fiction; its defence of a woman's right to write answers the attacks made on her in the theatre and the press.
literary_significance: It is a foundational document of women's literary self-representation and of the professional author's apology, and it remains the principal source for the biography of the early-eighteenth-century woman of letters.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work claims to be written by the person it reports, and the identification with the author of the secret history is made on its title-page.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1714 in octavo within a collected issue of the author's performances; modern readers use the scholarly reprint with collation of the variant title-pages.

title: The Busie Body
description: A city comedy of gossip, project and guardianship, the play that established its author as the most successful woman dramatist of the early eighteenth century. Its busy-bodies, a pair of meddling widows who superintend everyone's affairs, frame a plot of a fortune-hunting colonel, a ward and her several suitors.
plot_or_argument: An amorous colonel arrives in London resolved to make his court to a rich ward, and finds her guarded by two busy-body neighbours who report his designs and arrange her marriage to a fool. His servant and the ward's lovers counterplot, a ball and its gig of the age assemble the company, and the final division of the lady's property among three competitors exposes the arithmetic of the marriage market. The busy-bodies themselves are outwitted and reconciled to the younger pair.
narrative_structure: Five-act city comedy in prose and verse with a strictly interlocked main and underplot; the scenes of the busy-bodies' surveillance provide the comic engine and the division-of-property set piece the climax.
principal_characters: the two busy-body neighbours; the fortune-hunting colonel; his witty servant; the wealthy ward; her three competing suitors; the projectors of the age
literary_form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Brisk prose dialogue with the irregular mixture of verse passes usual in early-eighteenth-century comedy; the scenes run on quick repartee and the interruption of gossip.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1709 and frequently revived; the division-of-property scene was read aloud in the House of Commons in 1719 during the debate on the bill against patent projecting, a mark of how topical its satire on project and gossip had become.
literary_significance: It is the central instance of the post-Restoration city comedy rewritten for a Whig commercial audience, and a landmark in the history of women's professional playwriting; its treatment of female guardianship and of the price of an heiress anticipates the comic novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name and its success was registered in the pirated editions and revivals of the following decades.
bibliographical_notes: First performed in 1709 and printed in octavo in the same year, with reissues through the century; the standard critical text follows the first quarto with collation of the later acting versions.

title: The Wonder: A Woman Keeps a Secret
alternative_titles: The Wonder, A Woman Keeps a Secret
description: A comic drama of jealousy and female reticence, set in a Spanish-Portuguese court and its island, and the author's most popular play with the following generation of readers and managers. Its title phrase passed into proverb, and its heroine's refusal to explain her secret supplies the plot's mechanism.
plot_or_argument: A jealous governor suspects his sister's conduct and confines her, while a rival lover's designs on an heiress are pursued in the island scheme. The women keep their counsel through apparent betrayals, the men misread every signal, and the discovery of the secret clears the innocent and unites the lovers. The comedy ends with the governor's jealousy turned into an emblem of the sex's power over male inference.
narrative_structure: Five-act regular comedy in verse and prose, with a tightly interlocked intrigue of jealousy and a delayed revelation; the secret is structurally held until the fifth-act discovery.
principal_characters: Inez, the wondering woman; her brother the jealous governor; Caesario; Clara; Blazina; the rival gallants
literary_form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets mixed with prose for the lower scenes, in the post-Dryden comic manner; the repartee depends on balanced half-lines and the interruption of the couplet.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1714 and revived throughout the century, including in the altered version of the 1740s; its Spanish setting belongs to the vogue for Iberian comic scenes inherited from the Restoration.
literary_significance: It consolidated the comedy of female discretion as a civic virtue and became the stock example of a woman dramatist's command of regular construction; its proverbial title marks its penetration into everyday language.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name and was claimed for her in the biographical prefaces of the collected edition.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in octavo in 1714 following its stage success, with numerous later issues and an altered theatrical version in mid-century; the standard text follows the first quarto.

title: A Bold Stroke for a Wife
alternative_titles: A Bold Stroke for a Wife: A Comedy
description: The author's best-known comedy, a comic campaign in which a clever lover wins an heiress by personating the several guardians who have been charged with keeping her from him. It is a sustained satire on religious and political cant, each guardian standing for a species of enthusiasm.
plot_or_argument: A colonel loves a young woman whose fortune is controlled by four guardians, a Quaker, a nun, a Whig knight and a Tory general, each pledged to keep her from him. He and his friends disguise themselves as a Quaker preacher, a confessor and a petitioning politician, and by playing each guardian's own cant against him they obtain her consent. The exposure of the tricks reconciles the guardians and the lovers marry.
narrative_structure: Five-act comedy built on a single conceit of successive personation, with an epilogue and prologue addressing the party divisions of the house; the disguise scenes are arranged as set pieces of mimicry.
principal_characters: Colonel Fainwell; Miss Lovely; Obadiah Prim the Quaker; the nun Perpetua; Sir Simon Affection; the Tory general
literary_form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Predominantly prose dialogue with verse epilogue, the humour carried by the stylised cant of each guardian - Quaker plainness, Romish casistry, party phraseology.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1718, in the season of the Whig split and the Jacobite scare, and held a repertory place through the century; its portraits of Quaker and papist enthusiasts draw on the controversy comedy of the previous age.
literary_significance: It is the most durable English comedy about enthusiasm as a social language, and a central text for the study of the woman dramatist in the Augustan theatre; its personation structure was a model for later comedy of disguise.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name, though the pirated acting editions of the century alter its lines.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in octavo in 1718 soon after its first run, with frequent reissues and an altered version later in the century; the standard critical text follows the first edition.

title: Love in Excess; or, The Fatal Enquiry
alternative_titles: Love in Excess: Or, The Fatal Enquiry
description: The first and most ambitious of the amatory novels of its period, issued in parts over several years and built as a chain of interlaced histories of passion, seduction and betrayal. It sets the pattern of the long romance of the erring lover that its author afterwards dominated, and its tales of ruined women are narrated with a rhetoric of pity.
plot_or_argument: A young gentleman of fortune pursues an heiress and meets refusals, while in the tales within the narrative other lovers are tried by seduction, discovery and revenge. Brothers and rivals abduct, disguise and betray; women of condition are ruined by inquiry into their past, and the several histories converge through letters and unexpected recognitions. The closing parts resolve the errors by revelation of birth and the forgiveness of the offended.
narrative_structure: A serial multi-volume romance with embedded tales and a frame of continuous narration; the interlacing of stories is deliberate and the sequence of parts extends the suspense over years of publication.
literary_form: prose romance; amatory novel in several parts
meter_and_prosody: High romantic prose of apostrophe, exclamation and elaborated syntax, with letters and reported speeches; the style is consciously ornamented and emotionally intensified.
historical_context: Published in parts between 1719 and 1722 in the efflorescence of the three-volume romance, succeeding the translation-based fashion and competing directly with the scandalous fiction of the same booksellers.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of the amatory novel as a long form and the work that made its author the central female prose fiction-writer of the 1720s; its treatment of female complicity and male constancy shaped the genre down to the novelists of the 1740s.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the parts were published with the author's name after the success of the early issues, and she reissued the whole in revised form in the following decade.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in parts from 1719, the whole completed by 1722, in duodecimo and octavo issues; a revised edition appeared in the 1730s in a numbered three-volume format.

title: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze
alternative_titles: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze. By a Fine Lady
description: A short amatory tale in which a young woman, pursued no longer than she chooses to be, pursues a young officer by successive disguises, inventing for him one fictional person after another. It is the most praised of its author's fictions, a compact study of the masquerade of identity and of the economics of the sexual chase.
plot_or_argument: Seeing a young officer at a public exhibition, a lady of quality resolves to be enjoyed by him on her own terms; she lodges near him as a poor woman, is bought and resold by him, and then personates a wanton, a neighbour and finally a man to keep his desire alive. Each invention is exhausted and replaced by another until the last disguise, that of a rival male, forces him to flee the town; she then appears in her own person and renews the pursuit from the beginning.
narrative_structure: A single continuous third-person tale with a close ring composition: the last scene restores the first, so that the maze of the title is formally completed; the disguise episodes are arranged in escalating irony.
literary_form: short prose tale; amatory fiction
meter_and_prosody: Lucid, ironic prose with the free-indirect reporting of the heroine's calculations, and a rhetorical heightening borrowed from romantic diction but turned to comedy.
historical_context: Published in 1725 in a collected volume of the author's short fictions, in the season of the revival of the masquerade operas and of the controversy over the novel of intrigue; its own tale of disguise is a commentary on the theatre of the town.
literary_significance: It has been recovered as a masterpiece of early feminist narrative, its serial personation being read as an analysis of gender as performance and of the novel's own dependence on disguise.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published as by 'a fine lady' and gathered under the author's name in her collected fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1725 in octavo within a volume of short tales, and reprinted in the collected romances; it is now standardly read from the facsimile of that first issue.

title: The British Recluse
alternative_titles: The British Recluse: A Pastoral Romance
description: A short pastoral romance in which a retired lady and her companion recount the course of their loves in a cultivated English landscape. It is the author's deliberate domestication of the French heroic pastoral into English scenes, with songs and dialogues interspersed among the narrated histories.
plot_or_argument: Two gentlewomen, withdrawn from the town and its disappointments, pass their retirement in a British grove, where they tell and answer one another's histories of service, constancy and betrayal. Their own loves are reported in the manner of pastoral gallantry, trials of fidelity intervene, and the tales close in reconciliation rather than in tragedy. The frame presents retirement itself as the moral condition of the narrative.
narrative_structure: A framed pastoral with embedded tales and interspersed songs; the dialogue of the two narrators gives the sequence and the recessional structure of the romance.
literary_form: pastoral romance in prose with interspersed verse
meter_and_prosody: Ornamented romantic prose relieved by short lyric songs and dialogues in the conventional pastoral measures of the day.
historical_context: Published in 1728 in a volume issued with a comic opera adaptation, in the season of the pastoral revival and of the quarrel over the theatre's licentiousness; its retirement theme answers the town satire of the same years.
literary_significance: It shows the persistence of the heroic pastoral mode inside the emerging novel and is a document of the woman writer's control of the romance tradition, later reworked by the same hand in the novel of conduct.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the tale was gathered under the author's name in her collected fiction and reissued in the 1730s.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1728 in octavo, bound with a companion piece in a single volume; reprinted in the author's collected romances.

title: The Female Husband
description: A fictionalised life of the woman who passed as a man and married several women, published on the occasion of her trial at the Bristol court in 1746. It is a short scandalous biography in the Newgate manner, mixing report, invention and moral comment on the boundaries of sex and marriage.
plot_or_argument: A young person of masculine appearance and no fortune takes to the road in male dress, learns the practice of a physic, and courtships and marries women in several counties. The marriages are consummated or refused, the wives complain of deformity and distance, and the pursuit of an affectionate partner leads at last to detection, trial and punishment. The narrative reports the exposure with a mixture of sensational detail and professed moral horror.
narrative_structure: A continuous pseudo-biographical life in two short parts, following the trial report and the confessional narrative conventions of criminal biography; detection serves as the structural hinge.
principal_characters: the female husband; the successive brides; the constables and prosecutors; the Bristol court
literary_form: fictional biography and scandalous tale in prose
meter_and_prosody: Plain narrative prose with the abrupt, evidential sentences of the trial report and the raised register of the moral reflection.
historical_context: Published in 1746 out of the reports of a real prosecution for bigamy and deceit at the Bristol sessions, and in the same decade as the author's own conduct-oriented fiction; the case touched the law of marriage and the definition of sex.
literary_significance: It is a central text for the history of cross-dressing, gender impersonation and the legal fiction of sexual identity in eighteenth-century print culture, and evidence of the novelist's movement from amatory to documentary material.
attribution_notes: Attribution generally accepted on stylistic and publishing grounds and recorded as single; the text was published without the writer's name, and its subject is a real person whose own account differs.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1746 in two parts in octavo or duodecimo with a frontispiece; modern standard reading text is the scholarly facsimile of the first issue.

title: The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless
alternative_titles: The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless
description: A domestic novel in six volumes on the model of the conduct book, tracing a lively, vain young woman from an unprotected fortune through a bad marriage to a hard-won prudence. It is the author's fullest attempt to convert the amatory plot into a moral education and a deliberate address to the conduct of young women.
plot_or_argument: Betsy, orphaned and left to the guard of uncles and brothers, enjoys the flattery of admirers and the liberties of an unregulated spirit. Her brother's choice of a drunken husband for her proves ruinous; separation, attempted seduction, scandal and the intervention of a steadfast friend expose the danger of a woman's dependence on male protection. She earns at last the right to remarry well, the narrative closing on the lessons her suffering has taught.
narrative_structure: Continuous third-person narration in six volumes with didactic addresses to the reader; the plot is organised as a progression from thoughtlessness to discretion rather than as an intrigue.
literary_form: novel; domestic and conduct fiction in prose
meter_and_prosody: Plain narrative prose with a strongly intrusive narrator, apostrophes to the female reader and sententious closures; dialogue carries the social comedy.
historical_context: Published in 1751 in the season of the novelist's conduct turn and of the rival domestic fictions of the same decade, and drawing on the licensing debate and the new moral seriousness of the mid-century book trade.
literary_significance: It is the most complete of the early novels by a woman that reframes the seduction plot as an education in prudence, and an important link between the amatory romance of the 1720s and the later novel of female experience.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and reissued in the following decade.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1751 in six volumes in duodecimo; a later edition appeared in the 1760s, and the standard scholarly text follows the first issue.

title: Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded
alternative_titles: Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded. In a Series of Familiar Letters
description: A novel in letters and papers by a servant girl who defends her chastity against her young master and is finally rewarded with marriage into the gentry. It was written rapidly as a conduct example for servants and became the most discussed English prose fiction of the 1740s, generating answers, abridgements and imitations within months.
plot_or_argument: Pamela Andrews, fifteen and in service, is pursued by her master with escalating importunity, from trickery and surprise to attempted rape and imprisonment at his country house. She writes to her parents at every stage, resists the instruments of his design, escapes to her home and is recovered by him. After his reformation, effected by her rejection and by his own shame, he marries her; the second part reports her conduct as a wife and lady of the family.
narrative_structure: Epistolary and journal form, the letters written in the heat of the event and revised by the editor-narrator; the second part shifts to a retrospective domestic narrative with letters and papers.
principal_characters: Pamela Andrews; Mr. B; Mrs. Jervis; Mrs. Jewkes; Mr. Williams; the parson and the squire's mother; Jonathan
literary_form: epistolary novel in two parts
meter_and_prosody: A deliberately plain and idiomatic servant's prose, with the self-corrections of the writer-in-the-moment and a scriptural and proverbial tag; the elevated passages are reserved for the moral reflections.
historical_context: Composed in the winter of 1739-40 and published in the season that also saw the new Licensing Act, the novelist's own printer's shop supplying the material conditions of the book; its immediate imitations included a celebrated burlesque and a rival continuation.
literary_significance: It founded the epistolary novel of sexual danger and moral triumph in English and set the terms of the century's argument about fiction's instruction, from the critics of its detail to the defenders of its reward.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the design stated in the preface and defended by the author in the postscript and the following year's writing.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by the author and issued in London in 1740 in two volumes in duodecimo, with a third and fourth part in the same year; standard editions follow the first edition text with the variant issues noted.

title: Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady
alternative_titles: Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady. Written by a Fellow-Citizen to His Family
The History of Miss Clarissa Harlowe
description: The history of a young woman forced by her family toward an unloved husband, betrayed by the libertine she trusts and destroyed by his final outrage, written in a correspondence between the principals, their confidants and their gaolers. It is the longest and most ambitious English novel of the century and the supreme achievement of the epistolary form.
plot_or_argument: Clarissa Harlowe, courted by her brother's enemy Solmes under family compulsion, accepts the protection of Lovelace, who carries her to London and confines her in a house of ill fame. Her letters to Anna Howe tell of stratagem after stratagem, her flight from house to house, and at last of rape and poisoned resolution. She refuses to marry her ravisher, declines to plead to the world, and dies by a long and prepared consumption; Lovelace is killed in a duel abroad, and the family's avarice is left exposed.
narrative_structure: A correspondence of several hands arranged and edited by the surviving friend, with the narrator's interpolations; the plot is advanced by the uneven timing of letters, so that the reader is placed inside the delays of the post.
principal_characters: Clarissa Harlowe; Robert Lovelace; Anna Howe; James Harlowe; the brother and sisters of the family; Solmes; Mrs. Sinclair; the physicians and the alms-house of the ending
literary_form: epistolary novel in several volumes
meter_and_prosody: An elastic prose capable of many registers, from the quick colloquial idiom of Lovelace to the Latinate gravity of Clarissa's meditations; the letters' periodic syntax enacts the self-examination of the writers.
historical_context: Written over four years and published between 1747 and 1748, in the decade of the new divorce and seduction debate and of the printing of the author's own conduct and parliamentary work; the novel's legal detail assumes the property and marriage law of the period.
literary_significance: It is the central tragedy of the English novel and the chief literary argument of the eighteenth century about female consent, family authority and the sovereignty of the individual conscience; its afterlife in the paintings, abridgements and imitations of the following fifty years is unmatched.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the correspondence fiction of the preface is the author's own device and the composition is documented in his letters of the 1740s.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1748 in seven volumes in duodecimo, the issue dates of the volumes spanning the year, with a revised second edition in the same year; the standard scholarly text is a critical edition from the first and second editions.

title: The History of Sir Charles Grandison
alternative_titles: The History of Sir Charles Grandison. Written in a Series of Letters Between Some Respectable Persons
description: The third and least-tried epistolary novel of the series, a history of a perfect Christian gentleman and of the woman who might have married him, written partly in answer to the objection that the last hero had been a libertine. Its subject is the regulation of desire by honour within a family and a church.
plot_or_argument: Harriet Byron, an heiress of principled modesty, is pursued by Sir Charles Grandison, whose suit is delayed by an Italian entanglement and the obstinacy of his sister. A rival relation attempts to carry her off and to marry her by surprise, and a bigamous Italian nobleman complicates the design. The several letters of the family and the friends sort out the errors, and the novel ends with Harriet refusing the imperfect suitor and remaining a single exemplar of conduct.
narrative_structure: Epistolary narration by a circle of correspondents, with the heroine's letters framing a society rather than a single suspense; the Italian episodes slow the English plot and the ending is deliberately quiet.
principal_characters: Sir Charles Grandison; Harriet Byron; the Grandison family; Mrs. Selby and her spying cousin; the Italian nobleman; the friends of the correspondence
literary_form: epistolary novel in several volumes
meter_and_prosody: A polished and at times redundant prose of the polite letter, with the formal period and the moral tag; the variety of correspondents is marked by slight differences of idiom.
historical_context: Published in 1753 after several years of composition and documentary preparation, in the same parliamentary season as the Jewish Naturalisation bill, whose antisemitic street violence the novelist watched and which the novel's character of the Jewish physician reflects.
literary_significance: It is the most complete attempt of the century to write a novel of positive exemplarity, and its failure to satisfy the readers of Clarissa became a lasting case study in the limits of exemplary fiction; it also transmitted the novelist's method to later domestic fiction.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the composition and publication are documented in the author's correspondence of the period.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1753-4 in seven volumes in duodecimo, with a contemporary revised issue and early abridgements; a standard scholarly edition follows the first edition.

title: The Author's Farce
description: The first of the Haymarket comedies, a farce about a playwright, his patronage and his poverty, in which the author's own career is made the subject and the theatre is satirised from inside. It was performed by a small company of actors at the little theatre in the Haymarket and at once established the writer as a theatrical as well as a literary force.
plot_or_argument: A unsuccessful author of plays is tempted by his family and his friends to abandon the pen, and is courted by a printer and an alderman project who would employ his wit for money. A rival poet and a set of theatrical supernumeraries complicate his chances, and the action passes into a show within the show in which the persons of his own imagination appear and dispute their creation. The author's fortunes are finally settled by the exposure of the projects and by the applause of the audience he has courted.
narrative_structure: Two-act farce with an inserted burletta and a battle of the authors on the stage; the plot is a chain of theatrical situations rather than a regular intrigue, and the personation device carries the satire.
principal_characters: the author of the title; the printer and the projecting alderman; the rival poet; the family who press him to quit the pen; the actors and supernumeraries of the Haymarket company
literary_form: farce and comic afterpiece, with inserted musical entertainment
meter_and_prosody: Brisk prose dialogue with versified songs and the rhymed set pieces of the inserted show; the style is deliberately low and topical.
historical_context: Staged in the summer of 1730 at the little Haymarket theatre, in the season of the decay of the patent houses, the vogue for burletta and opera afterpieces, and the writer's own need for theatrical income; it answers the theatrical quarrels of the day and looks forward to the licensing bill of 1737.
literary_significance: It began the series of plays that made the author a manager-dramatist and supplied the model of the play about authorship and the literary marketplace; its project satire feeds directly into the later comic prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name after performance and recorded in the bills of the Haymarket season.
bibliographical_notes: First performed in 1730 and printed in octavo in the same year, with the altered edition following; the standard text follows the first edition with the run of the afterpiece noted.

title: The Tragedy of Tragedies; or, The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great
description: A burlesque tragedy on heroic subjects, in which the tiny hero of the old ballad is placed inside an exact parody of heroic verse, with its declamation, its mono-syllabic names and its catastrophes of absurd magnitude. It is the most sustained English exercise in tragicomical burlesque of the century and was revised into a two-act form with a dedication that became a manifesto.
plot_or_argument: Tom Thumb, in miniature and married to the queen, discovers his beloved's intrigue with a courtier and sends his rival on errands that end in death. King Arthur's court supplies the dignity, the giants and the fathers the ceremony, and the accumulating duels and poisonings grow past all probability. The finale buries nearly the whole cast, the survivors being left to moralise on the fragility of heroic design.
narrative_structure: A regular five-act burlesque tragedy in the heroic manner, reduced later to two acts, with the parody sustained scene by scene against the conventions of tragic structure; the deaths are stacked for cumulative effect.
principal_characters: Tom Thumb; King Arthur; Queen Huncamunca; Doodle; Grumio; Glumdalca; Meridanta
literary_form: burlesque tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets and the inflated blank verse of tragedy used exactly for nonsense, with the famous mono-syllabic names and the tautological similes of the high style.
historical_context: First played at the Haymarket in 1731 and revived in altered form at Drury Lane in 1737 with a prose dedication to the reader and a preface critical of contemporary tragedy; the season was one of heroic revival and of managerial dispute.
literary_significance: It is the classic English parody of heroic tragedy and a key document of the quarrel between the legitimate theatre and the little houses; its preface and dedication are primary statements of the comic theory later applied in the novels.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the revised edition of the late 1730s carries the author's name, prefatory matter and a dedication much debated as criticism.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1731 in octavo following performance, with the enlarged and altered edition of 1737 including the musical interlude; the standard scholarly text collates both.

title: Pasquin
description: A comedy in two scenes with a play within it, subtitled a hermophrodite piece because it is at once comedy and tragedy. Its declared design is to show that the stage may correct the age, and its target is the corruption of a court and a ministry by flattery and place-taking.
plot_or_argument: In the frame, a young lover of integrity is pressed by his friends to take a court position, and a wicked minister's designs on office and on the heroine are exposed. The inserted tragedy of the fair Virginia shows a virtuous subject destroyed by a tyranny, and its performance converts the spectators of the frame. The two plots together argue that the stage teaches by example, and the good are rewarded when the court's agents are unmasked.
narrative_structure: A frame comedy of two parts enclosing a short serious drama, the inserted play's moral function being explicitly argued in the dialogue; the structure is essayistic rather than intrigue-driven.
principal_characters: the honest young lover of the frame; the corrupt courtier and his dependants; the spectators of the inserted tragedy; the heroine of the inserted drama
literary_form: comic drama with inserted tragedy, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Prose in the frame and verse in the inserted tragedy, the two styles being contrasted to make the critical point about the genres' different powers.
historical_context: First performed at the little theatre in the Haymarket in March 1736, in the height of the Walpolean debate over the playhouse and the theatre's capacity for party attack, three months before the Lord Chamberlain's new censorship of 1737; the writer's theatre was among the institutions affected by it.
literary_significance: It is the most explicit statement in dramatic form of the century's argument for the stage as a school of public virtue, and a central document of the quarrel that produced the Licensing Act of 1737.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and advertised with a preface on the design of the piece.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1736 in octavo with the preface, and reprinted in the collected plays of 1737; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: Shamela
description: A short burlesque of the servant-girl novel, published anonymously in the same season as its original, which turns the heroine's letters into the devices of an artful seductress pursuing her aim. It is the earliest and sharpest of the answers to the conduct fiction, arguing from inside the form that its morality was interested.
plot_or_argument: Shamela Andrews, a country servant with an eye on her mistress's estate, writes letters home rehearsing her own arts of attack and defence. She is courted, resisted and finally complied with on her own schedule, her scruples being the scruples of design, and she secures a proposal from the squire while keeping the old woman and the parson in play. The piece ends with her married and in possession, the pretence of virtue having served the whole design.
narrative_structure: An epistolary burlesque in a single short volume, the letters' dates and self-exposures replacing the original's suspense; the prefatorial apparatus directs the reading as party attack.
principal_characters: Shamela Andrews; Squire Booby; Parson Williams; Mrs. Slipslop; the old lady of the family
literary_form: short epistolary burlesque and prose satire
meter_and_prosody: A debased copy of the servant style, with the idiom and misspellings of the original mocked and the candid sentences of the design breaking through the piety.
historical_context: Published in April 1741, three months after the conduct novel it answers, in a season crowded with its imitations and abridgements; the pamphlet war over the education of women and the price of virtue formed its immediate context.
literary_significance: It invented the technique of the ideologically inverted parody and remains the standard instance of the eighteenth-century argument that the novel of moral reward was a fiction of interest; it also led directly to the author's own theory of comic prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution long anonymous and established by internal evidence, the contemporary advertisement and later acknowledgment; recorded here as single.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1741 in duodecimo, without the author's name and with a preface to the author of Pamela; it is usually reprinted with the following year's comic preface.

title: Joseph Andrews
alternative_titles: The History of the Adventures of Joseph Andrews, and of His Friend Mr. Abraham Adams
description: A comic history of the road, the first English novel to announce itself as a comic epic poem in prose, following a footman and a poor scholar on their journeys out of and back into their master's house. Its prefatorial essay on the ridiculous supplied the age with its most used comic theory.
plot_or_argument: Joseph, a footman who keeps his chastity against his mistress's importunity, is turned out of the house and sets out to find his beloved Fanny. With his friend Mr. Adams, an absent but good-hearted parson, he travels by stage-coach, foot and waggon through a sequence of inns, beggars, gypsies, justices and physicians. Affection, hypocrisy and the affectation of virtue are exposed on the way, and the discovery that Joseph is Adams's future son-in-law by birth removes the last obstacle to the marriage.
narrative_structure: Third-person picaresque narration in book form with an intrusive narrator, digressory critical chapters and a discovery plot; the road supplies the sequence, the digressions the argument.
principal_characters: Joseph Andrews; Mr. Abraham Adams; Fanny Goodwill; Lady Booby; Mrs. Slipslop; the various innkeepers, justices and physicians of the road
literary_form: comic novel in prose, described as a comic epic poem
meter_and_prosody: A narrative prose of high comedy with the periodic digression of the critical chapters; the style takes up and exaggerates the diction of the romance and dramatic writers it holds up to burlesque.
historical_context: Written and published between the two Pamela-answer volumes of 1741-2, in the season of the war of the theatre and the new copyright debates; its theory of the ridiculous answers both the sentimental and the licentious vogue.
literary_significance: It created the self-conscious comic novel in English and set the terms of the century's debate about humour, affectation and the ridiculous, from its own prefatory essay to its later critics.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the first volume appeared in the author's name, and the prefatory essays are signed by the design of the work.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1742 in two volumes in duodecimo, with a revised edition in the following decade; standard scholarly editions follow the first edition with the variant prefaces.

title: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
description: The author's masterpiece and the most completely designed English novel of the century, the history of a foundling's education in good-nature and in error, from the country house of his benefactor through the road and the great city to the discovery of his birth. Each of its eighteen books opens with a chapter of critical preface.
plot_or_argument: Tom, an unknown child taken in by the wealthy Allworthy, grows up generous, hot-blooded and imprudent, and is opposed by the artful Blifil and instructed by the tutor Thwackum and Square. His love for Sophia is cross'd by her family's design on her for another; he is expelled, she runs away, and both travel to London by separate adventures. There Tom's errors culminate in an imprisonment and a near-execution, and the discovery that he is Allworthy's own sister's son clears his title to the estate and to Sophia.
narrative_structure: Eighteen books in three great movements - country, road, London - with a doubled chronology and an elaborate chain of discoveries; the prefatory chapters form a parallel argument on the writing of comic history.
principal_characters: Tom Jones; Squire Allworthy; Blifil; Sophia Western; Mrs. Western; Thwackum; Square; Lady Bellaston; Jenny Jones and her husband
literary_form: comic novel in prose, in the manner of a comic epic in eighteen books
meter_and_prosody: A commanding narrative prose of balanced period and pointed irony, capable of the colloquial energy of the road and the oratory of the prefatory essays; dialogue is sharply differentiated by class and profession.
historical_context: Composed after the author's marriage and during his essays on administration and society, and published in 1749 in the season of the riotous rejoicing over the peace and of the street disturbances which the novel's London scenes use.
literary_significance: It is the touchstone of the theory of the novel as a formally ordered art, its design and its analysis of good-nature and prudence setting the terms of discussion from the eighteenth century to modern criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in his correspondence and in the contemporary reviews.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1749 in six volumes in duodecimo, with revised issues in the author's lifetime; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition with collation of the later.

title: Amelia
description: The last and most serious of the comic histories, the story of a virtuous woman tried by her husband's imprudence, by debt and by the pursuit of a corrupt seducer. It abandons the road and the country house for the garrison, the fleet, the alehouse and the gaol, and is the most directly argumentative of the author's fictions.
plot_or_argument: Colonel Booth, an officer of honour and no prudence, marries Amelia against her guardian's will and carries her through the campaigns and stations of his career. His loss of money at the dice, his friendships with the designing, and the machinations of Bellers and of a lewd colonel bring him into arrest and Newgate. Amelia's conduct under every trial - seduction, bankruptcy, prison and the death of her child - converts her husband and exposes the laws and the customs that ruin good men, and the closing papers promise a recompense.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration in twelve books with a strong didactic current, framed by a prefatorial address to the fair sex and by an appendix of argument; the plot is a continuous trial rather than an intrigue.
principal_characters: Colonel Booth; Amelia Booth; William Bellers; Colonel James; Mrs. Patience; the gaolers and officers of Newgate
literary_form: novel; domestic and moral prose fiction in twelve books
meter_and_prosody: An earnest, periodic prose with the lawyer's and magistrate's precision in the passages of argument; the dialogue of the lower rooms is reported in a broad colloquial idiom.
historical_context: Published in 1751 by the author then a sitting magistrate at Bow Street, in the same season as his enquiry into robbers and the debate over the gin acts and the discipline of the metropolis; its law, finance and gaol detail come from official experience.
literary_significance: It is the eighteenth century's boldest attempt to make the novel an instrument of social reform and to place a good woman's suffering at the centre of its argument, and its cold reception marked the limit of the comic-history form.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in his correspondence of the last years.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1751 in six volumes in duodecimo, with a second edition the same year; standard editions follow the first edition.

title: An Enquiry into the Causes of the Late Increase of Robbers
alternative_titles: An Enquiry into the Causes of the Late Increase of Robbers, and Other Disorders of the Present Times
An Enquiry into the Late Increase of Robbers
description: A magistrate's enquiry into the disorder of the metropolis, occasioned by the observations made in a late riot trial and arguing that the increase of robbers follows from the diffusion of gin, the decay of the moral restraint of the poor and the failure of the laws. It is the most influential of the criminal-enquiry pamphlets of the mid-century.
plot_or_argument: The writer examines the causes of the late growth of street robbery and riot, laying the first weight on the spirit trade and the gin houses, then on the dissolution of family and apprenticeship discipline, the idleness of Journeymen, and the corruption of the constables and the watch. He compares the severity and the execution of the existing laws, and argues that the theater and the price of admission spread the same loose principles. His remedies are regulation of the spirits, better police, and the restraint of the common plays.
narrative_structure: A single continuous argument in numbered sections, each cause being stated, illustrated from the office books and answered against objection; the pamphlet closes with proposals rather than a conclusion.
literary_form: public enquiry and policy pamphlet in prose
meter_and_prosody: Clear magistrate's prose of instance and enumeration, with the periodic sentence of the argumentative close and frequent appeal to reported fact.
historical_context: Written from the Bow Street office in the spring of 1751 during the debates on the Gin Act and after the Covent Garden riot over the price of seats at Drury Lane, an event the pamphlet treats directly.
literary_significance: It is a primary document of the century's urban policing and social investigation, and it supplies the professional basis of the novelist's later fictions of the metropolis; its analysis of pleasure, drink and disorder shaped reform argument for a generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name as a sitting magistrate and reprinted in his collected tracts.
