bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1751, in a short quarto or octavo pamphlet with several issues in the same year and enlargements in later editions; standard discussion follows the first issue with the additions noted.

title: A Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
alternative_titles: The Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
description: The account of a dying man's sea passage, written by an author who sailed for Lisbon in the hope of health and died on the way home. It mixes the journal of the voyage, the complaint of the ship's company and a serious meditation on the conduct of a physician and the resignation of a man who expects to die.
plot_or_argument: The traveller, broken by illness and obliged to leave England, describes his departure, the passage and his sufferings on board, with the behaviour of his own family and of the other passengers under the same trial. He reports the quarrels, the sickness, the crew and the treatment of the sick by the ship's surgeon, arriving at Lisbon in a condition little amended. The journal closes with the return homeward and the traveller's death, which the publishers' advertisement disclosed.
narrative_structure: A dated prose journal of a single crossing, continuous in its observation and rising to a set of reflective conclusions on sickness, death and the duties of those who attend them.
principal_characters: the travelling author; his wife and attendants; the ship's company and the surgeon; the fellow passengers of the Lisbon packet
literary_form: travel journal and personal narrative in prose
meter_and_prosody: A plain diary prose of the daily entry, with the heightened periodic manner reserved for the closing meditations on death.
historical_context: Written in the autumn of 1754 and published a few months after the author's death in Lisbon in October of that year, in the season of his retirement from the office and of the controversy over his conduct as a magistrate.
literary_significance: It is the most affecting of the century's dying autobiographies and a crucial companion to the fiction, its candid account of the body and of domestic weakness confirming the argument of the last novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published posthumously from the writer's own journal, with a prefatorial advertisement of the circumstances of his death.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1755 in octavo or duodecimo with advertisements, and reprinted in the collected works; the text is stable and modern editions follow the first issue.

title: The History of the Adventures of David Simple
description: The history of a young man of good nature who trusts the world to be like himself, written by a novelist who set out to improve the moral fiction of her brother's school by making sensibility the subject rather than the instrument. Its design is to show how an honest and credulous heart is tried by interest and flattery.
plot_or_argument: David Simple, disinherited by a father's second marriage and thrown upon his own fortune, travels and lodges among a succession of friends and impostors, each testing his generosity. He is imposed upon by designing relations, tried by a false friendship and rewarded by a faithful one, and his sister's and his own loves are disentangled by discoveries. The narrative ends with the good established and the worldly exposed, the moral being that benevolence requires judgement.
narrative_structure: Third-person episodic narration with a strong exemplary frame, the episodes arranged as trials of David's trust; dialogue carries most of the moral argument.
principal_characters: David Simple; his brother and his sister; the false friend and the true; the designing relations and the tried lovers
literary_form: novel; sentimental and exemplary prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: An artless and colloquial prose, modelled on conversation and on the plain style, with the didactic summary at the close of the scene.
historical_context: Published in 1743 in the season immediately following the comic histories, and written within the author's own family circle; the novel's theory of good nature answers the selfish-system philosophy then under debate.
literary_significance: It is an early and influential statement of the cult of good nature in the novel, and one of the first English fictions to make a benevolent man's disappointment in the world its governing interest.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was published without a name at the first issue but was acknowledged within the family circle and by advertisement.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1743 in two volumes in duodecimo, with a second edition soon following; the sequel volume was issued separately and the two are now usually read together.

title: Volume the Last
alternative_titles: The History of the Adventures of David Simple. Volume the Last
description: The continuation and reversal of the first history of David Simple, in which the exemplary reward given to good nature in the earlier volume is withdrawn and the world's punishment of it is shown in earnest. It is a darker and more experimental book, much praised by later readers for its honesty about disappointment.
plot_or_argument: David, now settled in a family and a fortune of his own, is successively stripped of what he loved: his wife dies, his children are taken or lost, and his property is engrossed by a fraudulent relation. The friends who were promised by the first volume fail him, and the closing books report his decline into poverty and death. The tale ends with an address on the condition of the good in a world governed by interest.
narrative_structure: A continuous third-person narrative in twelve books, structured as a progressive bereavement rather than an intrigue; the ending refuses closure and turns to direct moral address.
principal_characters: David Simple; his wife and children; the fraudulent relation and the law officers; the failing friends of the first volume
literary_form: novel; sentimental fiction in twelve books
meter_and_prosody: A plainer and more compressed prose than the first volume, with the pathos carried by short report and by the narrator's restrained comment.
historical_context: Published in 1747 after some years of retirement from print, in the season of the author's own editorial and translation work and of the mid-century debate about the instruction of novels.
literary_significance: It is an early and striking instance of the anti-exemplary novel, its reversal of the rewards of virtue being read as a critique of the sentimental plot and of the conduct tradition.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested, established by the family circle's records and by the continuity of person and design with the earlier volume.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1747 in two volumes in duodecimo as the concluding volume of the former history; long neglected and reprinted by modern scholars.

title: The Governess; or, Little Female Academy
description: A story of a boarding school for girls, in which a wise governess governs by letting her pupils tell and judge one another's tales. It is the first English book written deliberately for the entertainment and instruction of girls of that age, and a foundation text of the children's novel.
plot_or_argument: Ten or eleven girls arrive at the academy, each with her own fault of temper, vanity or falsehood, and the governess discovers their characters by observation rather than by rule. The girls are set to tell stories of their own invention - tales of lovers, of servants and of the adventures of the world - and to pass judgement on one another's conduct. The book closes with the reformation of the stubborn and the reward of the modest, the governess's method having turned amusement into moral discipline.
narrative_structure: A framed collection: a continuous school narrative enclosing tales told by the pupils, the frame supplying the judgement and the tales the example; the sequence is orderly and episodic.
principal_characters: the governess of the academy and her pupils, each standing for a fault or a virtue of temper
literary_form: children's fiction; framed school story with embedded tales
meter_and_prosody: Simple conversational prose suited to young readers, with the inset tales adopting the diction of the popular romance they parody.
historical_context: Published in 1749, in the season of new attention to the education of girls and of the didactic tales of the day, and written by an author already associated with conduct-oriented fiction and school teaching.
literary_significance: It invented the English school story for girls and is a landmark in the history of a literature designed for female childhood, influencing the didactic fiction of the following century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and with a preface addressed to the parents of the pupils.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1749 in duodecimo with plates, and reprinted many times in the 1750s and 1760s, including in improved editions; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition.

title: The Life of Harriot Stuart
alternative_titles: The Life of Harriot Stuart, Written by Herself
description: A first-person history of a young woman of quality carried by seduction, elopement and war from England to America and back. It was the author's first novel and an immediate success, combining the amatory plot with a self-conscious criticism of the romances its heroine has read.
plot_or_argument: Harriot Stuart, the daughter of a noble family, is courted by designing men, betrayed by one who pretends to honour and pursued through a forced journey to the colonies. Her lover follows her across the Atlantic, the two are caught in the frontier war, and an elopement and a second seduction plot bring them within reach of ruin. Recovery and marriage come only after the exposures, and the narrative closes on the lesson that a woman's judgement must govern her sensibility.
narrative_structure: Continuous first-person retrospect in two volumes, the American sections supplying a picaresque and military interlude inside the amatory design; letters and reported speeches carry the crisis.
principal_characters: Harriot Stuart; the false suitor of her English years; her faithful lover; the officers and settlers of the American sections
literary_form: novel; amatory and autobiographical prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: A fluently emotional prose of the confessional style, with the heightened address of the romantic tradition moderated by ironic self-commentary.
historical_context: Published in 1750, in the season of the mid-century vogue for histories written by themselves and of the colonial material drawn from the war in America; its author, a woman of the Bluestocking world, followed it with a series of novels and critical work.
literary_significance: It is an important early instance of the novel that both uses and examines the amatory plot, and it established its author as one of the professional women novelists of the mid-century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the collected editions of her works.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1750 in two volumes in duodecimo, with a second edition in the same year; standard scholarly editions follow the first.

title: The Female Quixote; or, The Adventures of Arabella
description: The comedy of a young heiress who, having read nothing but romances, governs her conduct by their laws and reads every man as a knight and every civility as a homage. It is the most sustained English treatment of the madwoman of the reading plot and one of the century's central statements about fiction's power over its readers.
plot_or_argument: Arabella, beautiful and rich, insists upon the ceremonious courtship prescribed by the romances and refuses the plain addresses of the man she ought to marry. Her lover and her friend try various devices to cure her, including a counter-romantic treatment which makes her believe herself admired in the old style. The exposure of a designing admirer at last breaks the illusion, and the closing reconciliation is effected by a physician who prescribes history and religion against romance.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration in two volumes, the plot a single sustained irony maintained by the heroine's misreadings; the episodes are arranged as trials of her interpretive system and resolved by an anti-romance cure.
principal_characters: Arabella; her lover and friend; the designing admirer who works on her delusion; the physician and the moralist of the conclusion
literary_form: comic novel; moralities of reading in prose
meter_and_prosody: A clear ironic prose that quotes and parodies the diction of the heroic romance in the heroine's speeches, the comedy lying in the mismatch of registers.
historical_context: Published in 1752, in the season of the quarrel over the danger of novel-reading and of the author's own friendship with the leading writers of the day, including the lexicographer who advertised the book; its target includes the surviving vogue of translated romance.
literary_significance: It gave the century its most influential figure of the female reader corrupted by fiction and supplied the model for later treatments of romantic delusion, from its own imitators to the nineteenth-century novel of reading.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and long, wrongly, credited to another hand by early bibliographers before being firmly reassigned.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1752 in two volumes in duodecimo, with many reissues and translations; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition.

title: Henrietta
description: A novel of a portionless young woman, a poor relation in a great house, whose virtue is tried by presumption, by a fraudulent seduction and by the world's readiness to believe the worst of a woman alone. It is darker and more analytical than the author's earlier fiction and much concerned with the opinion of the world as a tribunal.
plot_or_argument: Henrietta, dependent on relations of consequence, is pursued by a man of fortune who offers protection rather than marriage, and later by one whose design is outright seduction. She defends herself with spirit, is compromised in appearance, and must bear the verdict of society while the men who injured her are spared. Her constancy and the exposure of her persecutors prepare a marriage on equal terms, the narrative arguing that a woman's reputation is a social construction.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration in two volumes with a strong current of moral essay; the plot turns on the difference between Henrietta's conduct and the world's report of it.
principal_characters: Henrietta; her protectress and the great family; the two pursuers, one coarse and one designing; the suitor who finally offers equality
literary_form: novel; domestic and moral prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: An argentine prose of reflection and reported conversation, with the narrator's essays on female dependency interrupting the narrative.
historical_context: Published in 1758, in the decade of the mid-century novel's turn to the analysis of reputation and dependency, and after the author's critical work on the drama had fixed her place in letters.
literary_significance: It is one of the most acute mid-century analyses of the sexual double standard in fiction and a key text in the development of the novel of the unprotected woman.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1758 in two volumes in duodecimo; reissued in the collected editions of the author's works.

title: Shakespear Illustrated
alternative_titles: Shakespear Illustrated: Containing the Genuine Plot of His Best Plays, Proving That They Are Translations from the Italian, Spanish and French
Shakespear Illustrated, with Essays Proving His Plays Translations
description: A critical collection proving from the antecedent tales that the plots of Shakespeare's best plays are borrowed from Italian, Spanish and French originals, each play being faced with an abstract of the source. Its prefatory discourse on the properties of drama is an early statement of neoclassical plot doctrine in English criticism.
plot_or_argument: The work examines a sequence of the plays - among them Othello, Measure for Measure, All's Well That Ends Well, Romeo and Juliet and The Taming of the Shrew - and sets against each the story Shakespeare found. It shows the plot as given, the alterations as made, and argues that the poet's judgement rather than his invention is to be praised or blamed. The prefatory discourse draws the conclusion that fidelity to probability and to the unities is the measure of dramatic merit.
narrative_structure: A series of comparative essays, each pairing an abstract of the source with remarks on the play, framed by a general discourse on the drama; the argument is cumulative and evidential.
literary_form: critical treatise with comparative abstracts of sources
meter_and_prosody: Plain argumentative prose of the mid-century critical essay, with the quoted abstracts in a deliberately bald narrative style.
historical_context: Published in 1753 in two volumes, in the season of the great editions of Shakespeare and of the quarrel over his regularity, and written by a novelist-critic with access to the Italian and Spanish sources through translation.
literary_significance: It is an important document of source study before scholarship and of the eighteenth-century argument about Shakespeare's obligations to the romance tradition, anticipating later source criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, though early bibliographers occasionally misassigned it.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1753 in two volumes in octavo or duodecimo; no modern complete edition is standard, and the work is usually cited from the first issue.

title: The Adventures of Roderick Random
description: A picaresque novel in two volumes, the history of a disinherited Scottish boy who runs to sea, survives the South Seas station and the West India fleet, and works his way in England and Jamaica to the recovery of his fortune and the discovery of his family. Its note of personal grievance and its command of low life made it an immediate success.
plot_or_argument: Roderick Random, expelled from his grandfather's house and beaten at school, sails as a surgeon's mate in a man-of-war and endures the brutality of the captains, the sickliness of the station and the horrors of a West India voyage. He deserts, fights, is wrecked, and reaches Jamaica, where he accumulates money and connections. In London he is seduced into debt and marriage by a designing woman, but a series of discoveries restores his estate, his father's name and his friend's fortune, and the tale ends in the marriages of the good.
narrative_structure: First-person picaresque in two volumes, a continuous chain of adventures ordered by the hero's progress upward; the sea books are tightly documented and the English books looser and more satirical.
principal_characters: Roderick Random; Andrew Strap, his friend; the grandfather and the relations who wrong him; the ship's surgeons, captains and mates of the navy; the designing woman of the London books
literary_form: picaresque novel in prose
meter_and_prosody: A vigorous colloquial first-person prose, abundant in cant, Scots and naval vocabulary, with the sustained invective passage as its characteristic unit.
historical_context: Published in 1748 after the author's own medical and naval service and his London editorial work, in the season of the close of the war of the Austrian succession and of public inquiry into the sick and wounded seamen; its navy scenes draw on report and experience.
literary_significance: It revived the picaresque in English with an unprecedented documentary force and made the Caribbean and the naval service central to the novel's geography; its political and professional satire shaped the later careers of the writer.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and advertised as the work of the editor of a periodical history.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1748 in two volumes in octavo, with a second and revised edition in the same year; the standard scholarly text collates the early editions.

title: The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle
description: The history of a young man of fortune from his mischief in a Scottish school through the sea, the tour, the stage and the King's Bench, to a reformation engineered by his faithful friend. It is the most various of the picaresque sequences, containing the century's most famous comic set pieces.
plot_or_argument: Peregrine, the son of a Lancashire family, is bound apprentice to a sea captain, runs away, and passes his youth in mischief and gambling. His guardians plot to ruin him for his estate, but his uncle intercepts their design and secures his estate; he travels in France, is seduced and seduces, keeps a mistress and a house, and turns to politics and the stage. His cruelty to a woman he has wronged and his duelling bring him to the prison and to death-bed penitence, before a final reconciliation and marriage.
narrative_structure: First-person-adjacent picaresque narration in volumes, the episodes grouped by place - school, ship, house, France, London - with the friend's loyalty supplying the moral continuity; the famous embedded tales interrupt the sequence.
principal_characters: Peregrine Pickle; his uncle the commodore; the two designing guardians; the faithful friend of the ship; the French mistress and the injured woman of the London books
literary_form: picaresque novel in prose
meter_and_prosody: A rowdy and various prose of caricature and ventriloquism, from the commodore's nautical thunder to the cant of the convent and the stage; the set pieces are comic declamation.
historical_context: Published in 1751 after the success of the first novel and the author's editorial warfare of the late 1740s, in the season of the Jewish Naturalisation bill's street agitation and of the arguments about French and popish customs which the book exploits.
literary_significance: It fixed the picaresque at its most energetic in English and supplied the age's most quoted comic tableaux; its treatment of the repentant rake made it a station on the road from the amatory to the sentimental novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, with later issues revised in the 1760s.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1751 in four volumes in octavo, with a much-altered edition in 1760s issues; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition with the variant passages.

title: The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom
alternative_titles: The Adventures of Ferdinand, Count Fathom
description: The history of a complete villain, a foundling instructed in every cheat who rises by forgery, bigamy, gambling and war into a title and an estate. It was offered in a prefatory advertisement as a defence of the regular novel against the charge of exceeding probability, and it is the most methodically wicked of the century's heroes.
plot_or_argument: Ferdinand, the son of a gypsy and a cheat and educated by a fencing master, is expelled from his patron's house after an intrigue and turns to the gaming and betting stages of Europe. He follows an army in Italy, is made a count by a deception on a noble house, and marries into wealth by the double fraud of two sisters. His crimes prosper almost unchecked until the last pages, when the exposure of his person and history reduces him to penury and a professed repentance.
narrative_structure: Continuous third-person narration of a single career in volumes, the episodes organised as the successive schools of villany; the prefatory argument on probability frames the design rather than interrupting it.
principal_characters: Ferdinand Count Fathom; his fencing-master and patron; the dupe noble family of Italy; the two sisters he deceives; the gamblers and camp-followers of his education
literary_form: picaresque novel with a villain-hero
meter_and_prosody: A hard, latinate and economical prose of the case and the contrivance, without the colloquial warmth of the earlier histories; the irony is reported rather than voiced.
historical_context: Published in 1753 after the author's return from France and his editorial labours, in the season of the debate on the novel's morality and of the new attention to the law of fraud and marriage which the plot exploits.
literary_significance: It is the century's most sustained attempt to make a professedly wicked life the subject of regular fiction, and its advertisement stands as an early statement of the theory of the novel as a structure of probable incidents.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1753 in three volumes in duodecimo, with reissues and a revised edition later; standard texts follow the first edition.

title: The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves
description: A short novel on the Quixote plan, in which an honest country knight of the mid-century, mad on the romances of chivalry, rides out to redress grievances in a Suffolk town. It was published in monthly numbers in a periodical before appearing in book form, and its comedy lies in the collision of an archaic code with a commercial county.
plot_or_argument: Sir Launcelot, having read nothing but romances, arms himself and sallies forth to right the wrongs of the neighbourhood, taking a squire and a doctor with him. He is set upon by creditors, justices and the retainers of a rival family, and his adventures end in beating and confinement rather than in conquest. His cause finally prevails by the intervention of his friends and by the exposure of the combinations that had oppressed the poor, and the book ends with the knight restored to his senses and his estate.
narrative_structure: A serially published short novel of monthly parts, the episodes arranged as a sequence of mishaps answering the romance structure; the periodical origin makes the numbers tight and the irony economical.
principal_characters: Sir Launcelot Greaves; his squire and his physician; the justice and the designing family who oppose him; the creditors and the tenantry of the county
literary_form: short comic novel in the Quixote tradition
meter_and_prosody: A dry and compressed prose of dialogue and report, the chivalric phrases of the hero set against the plain idiom of his attendants.
historical_context: Issued in numbers in a monthly magazine between 1760 and 1762, during the author's editorship of periodical work and the war-season enthusiasm and party heat that the book gently satirises; the romantic madness theme answers the Gothic vogue beginning in the same years.
literary_significance: It is the subtlest of the century's English Quixotes and an important document of the serialization of fiction in periodicals, anticipating the later short comic novel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name in the magazine and in the collected edition of his novels.
bibliographical_notes: First published in monthly numbers in a periodical from 1760, and collected in book form in 1762 in duodecimo volumes; the standard text follows the magazine numbers with the book issues collated.

title: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker
alternative_titles: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker. In a Series of Letters
description: The account of a family tour through England and Scotland, given in letters by five correspondents whose temperaments make the same scenes appear as five different books. It is at once the century's most successful comic novel of opinion, a handbook of the bath, road and fishery, and a study in the politics, medicine and morals of the late Georgians.
plot_or_argument: An old bachelor of fortune, his maiden aunt, his ward and their two servants set out for the waters at Bath and travel by Bristol, Wales, Liverpool and the Scottish Highlands home to London. Each correspondent reports the places and the people - the pump-room, the manufacturers, the Highland hospitality, the electors and the mobs - according to his or her interest, and the servants' own histories turn out to matter. Humphry Clinker is discovered to be an heiress's lost lover, the aunt is married against her principle of scorn, and the invalid is cured by the journey.
narrative_structure: A correspondence in five hands, arranged so that the same events are reported at a distance by different letters; the plot is carried by the delayed recognition of the servants' histories.
principal_characters: Matthew Bramble Esq.; his sister Tabitha; their ward and nephew; Humphry Clinker the footman-gardener; Mrs. Winifred Jenkins; the assistant of the Scottish journey
literary_form: epistolary novel of travel and opinion
meter_and_prosody: Five sharply distinguished prose idioms - the politer satiric period, the fussy feminine epistle, the young man's essay, the servant's blundering record - the comedy arising from their collision over a single fact.
historical_context: Written in the last years of the author's life at Nice and in London, and published in 1771, in the season of the heated politics of the Middlesex election and its riots, of the craze for the waters and for the Scottish tour, and of the debate on emigration and the fishery.
literary_significance: It is the richest of the eighteenth-century comic novels and the standard literary source for the geography of Georgian taste, reform and travel; its plural correspondence method was much imitated and remains a touchstone of narrative theory.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in the letters of its composition.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1771 in three volumes in duodecimo, with many reissues and the author's later revised text; the standard scholarly edition follows the first edition.

title: A Journey Through France and Italy
alternative_titles: A Journey Through France and Italy, in a Series of Letters
description: A book of travels in letters from an English invalid travelling with his family through France into the north of Italy, written during a residence abroad and published some years after the writer's death. It mixes the guidebook, the medical complaint and the moral essay, and is one of the most readable of the century's continental tours.
plot_or_argument: The traveller conducts his family from Dover through France, complains of the posts, the inns, the cooks and the beggars, and praises the laws and the politeness that make travelling easy. He enters Italy by Genoa and passes to Pisa and Livorno, where the climate and the medical advice are weighed; the letters report the companies, the opera and the antiquities. The final part recommends the Italian residence to consumptive English patients and judges the nations by their accommodation of the sick.
narrative_structure: A continuous series of letters arranged by route, with digressions on commerce, government, medicine and taste; the itinerary supplies the order and the invalid's temper the unity.
principal_characters: the travelling invalid and his family; the physicians and the innkeepers; the companies of the waters and of the opera
literary_form: travel narrative in letters
meter_and_prosody: A testy and idiomatic epistolary prose, with the enumerative energy of the complaint and the balanced manner of the political observation.
historical_context: Composed during the author's residence at Nice in the years after the peace of 1763, and published posthumously in 1776 in the season of the vogue for the Italian tour and the health-travel of the English.
literary_significance: It stands with the great travel books of the century as a document of the continental tour and of the medical geography of exile, and it supplies the circumstances of the author's last years.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after his death from his own letters and papers.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1776 in two volumes in octavo, with several reissues; the text is stable and standard reading editions follow the first.

title: The History of England (Smollett)
alternative_titles: The History of England, from the First Accession of James the Second to the Treaty of Chatellerault
description: A multi-volume narrative history of England from the Revolution of 1688 to the middle of the eighteenth century, undertaken as a commercial compilation and executed with a historian's argument about party, commerce and national character. It was the standard readable English history of the 1760s and 1770s and was several times revised and continued by the writer.
plot_or_argument: The work narrates the reigns and ministries from James II to the peace of 1763, attending to the settlement of the constitution, the wars, the funds and the parties. It judges the Toleration and the Revolution in a Tory-Whig middle register, dwells on the '45 and on the administration of the elder minister, and treats the growth of trade and credit as the true subject of the age. The later volumes and continuations carry the story into the author's own decade.
narrative_structure: A regular chronological narrative in volumes with periodic continuations and revised issues; the books are organised by reign and administration, with inserted character sketches and constitutional remarks.
principal_characters: James II; William III; the ministers and commanders of the wars; the pretender and the '45; the party leaders of the Hanoverian age
literary_form: narrative national history
meter_and_prosody: A sententious and rhetorical historical prose, closer to the manner of the Augustan historians than to the documentary school, with the balanced period of judgment as its characteristic unit.
historical_context: Written as a bookseller's speculation out of the earlier histories and the printed sources of the day, and published volume by volume in the years of the Seven Years' War, when the demand for a readable national history was acute and the party press still argued over the Revolution settlement.
literary_significance: It shows the eighteenth-century novelists' command of the philosophy of history and supplied a generation with its narrative of the recent past; its judgments on liberty, faction and commerce are a document of the Scottish and English historical thought of the mid-century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, though the work was largely composed from earlier histories, a practice then normal and afterwards criticised.
bibliographical_notes: The volumes appeared in London between 1757 and 1765 in octavo, with revised and continued issues; the precise date of each volume and of the original plan is not asserted here beyond the span of publication.

title: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
alternative_titles: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy
description: A gentleman's life and opinions, begun before his birth and never arriving at it, in which the telling of a life is interrupted by the machinery of telling. Its first two volumes were published together in 1759 and the series ran to nine, with the writing and the reader's impatience forming the true subject.
plot_or_argument: Tristram undertakes to write his life but is driven back to his father's theories of education, his uncle Toby's sieges and the misfortunes of his own naming and circumcising. The events of a Shandean life - the marriages, the wars, the errors of the midwife and of the post - are endlessly displaced by digression, while Yorick, the widow Wadman, Uncle Toby and Trim the horse supply their own episodes. The narrative advances by association and by the reader's expectation, closing in volumes that grow shorter and more reflective.
narrative_structure: A digressive and self-referential first-person narration in nine books, with marbled pages, a blank page and a page of arms; the plot is the impossibility of its own chronological telling.
principal_characters: Tristram Shandy; Walter Shandy, his father; Uncle Toby; Corporal Trim; Yorick; Dr. Slop; Susannah and the women of the house
literary_form: comic novel; experiment in narrative digression
meter_and_prosody: A prose of extraordinary rhythmic variety, from the aphoristic period of the projects to the broken colloquy of the kitchen, with the silence and the typographic device treated as parts of the style.
historical_context: Written by a Yorkshire clergyman and published from 1759 in London after a provincial start, in the season of the new sensibility, the lockean science of ideas and the quarrel over the novel's licence; its publication history is bound up with the author's own delay and revision.
literary_significance: It is the most radical narrative experiment of the century and a founding text of modern self-conscious fiction, anticipated by the readers of postmodernism and central to the history of the novel's idea of time.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, with the later volumes withdrawn and revised in issues that include the sermons' material.
bibliographical_notes: The first two volumes appeared in 1759, with the remaining volumes following between 1760 and 1767 in duodecimo; the standard scholarly text collates the early issues and reproduces the printed devices.

title: A Political Romance
description: A short squib on the politics of the northern church, in which the possessions and dignities of a see are represented as a family estate disputed by greedy relations. It was printed privately and suppressed almost at once, and its suppression is the best-documented quarrel of the author's Yorkshire years.
plot_or_argument: The affairs of an ancient manor and its offices are thrown into confusion by the designs of a steward and a faction of dependants, who would divide the profits and dispose of the lady of the house. The several parties plead their rights in a style of mock-legal and romantic gallantry, until the whole scheme is exposed as a traffic in dignities. The tale ends in the defeat of the project and in an ironical apology to the offended readers.
narrative_structure: A brief continuous allegorical tale in the romantic and lawyerly manner, the persons standing transparently for the parties of the diocese; the design is a single sustained joke of personation.
principal_characters: the personated dignitaries of the northern church; the scheming steward and his faction; the lady of the manor and her dependants
literary_form: allegorical prose satire and political squib
meter_and_prosody: A dense parodic prose of the romantic and the conveyancing styles, with the personated legal phrases of the real quarrel reproduced for effect.
historical_context: Written in 1759 in the heat of the dispute over the York diocesan offices and the family interests of the author's own circle, and withdrawn by the printer after threats of an action for scandal; the affair is recorded in the letters of the year.
literary_significance: It is the earliest publication of the author and the key to the personal and ecclesiastical material that later surfaces in the fiction, and its suppression is a case study in the practical limits of Augustan libel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; printed without the author's name and identified in his correspondence and by the parties attacked.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1759 in a short quarto, suppressed and largely destroyed, so that surviving copies are rare; modern readers use a reprint from one of the few remaining copies.

title: The Sermons of Mr. Yorick
alternative_titles: Sermons, by the Late Mr. Yorick
description: A collection of parish sermons published under the name of the fictional clergyman whose life the novels also report, and running to several volumes over the middle years of the decade. They are sermons of the conscience and of the passions, on temperance, on the nature of religious consolation, on the duty of mirth and on the danger of a hard heart.
plot_or_argument: The discourses examine the religious emotions of ordinary people, pressing on their hearers the duty of open-heartedness and the sin of the self-flattering hearer. They treat the love of pleasure, the neglect of the afflicted, the temper of a winter evening and the use of religious melancholy. The argument is not doctrinal but diagnostic, aiming to persuade the conscience by the analysis of its own feelings.
narrative_structure: A serial collection of printed sermons, each a short regular discourse with text, improvement and application, gathered into volumes with the persona of the preacher supplying the frame.
principal_characters: Mr. Yorick as the preaching persona; the parish audience; the afflicted and the self-deceived of the instances
literary_form: sermons and practical moral divinity
meter_and_prosody: A spoken prose of the pulpit of the day, with the short sentence of application, the rhetorical question and the tender parenthesis; the cadence is deliberately colloquial and moving.
historical_context: Published between 1760 and 1767 by a country clergyman who was simultaneously a fashionable writer, in the season of the sensible sermon and of the argument with enthusiasm, and often sold in numbers of the same bookseller as the fiction.
literary_significance: It supplies the serious underside of the author's reputation and is evidence of how the culture of feeling was worked through in the established church; several of the discourses were separately reprinted and translated.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volumes carry the pseudonymous preacher's name and are documented in the author's correspondence, though the persona occasionally disguises the hand.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in several volumes between 1760 and 1767 in duodecimo and octavo, with reissues and separate printings of individual sermons; the numbering of the volumes varies between the issues.

title: A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy
alternative_titles: The Sentimental Journey through France and Italy
description: The journal of a clergyman travelling in France and Italy with nothing but his feelings for an equipment, a book of episodes in which the encounter, not the place, is the subject. It gave the century the word sentimental in its modern sense and made the traveller's sympathetic alarm a literary form.
plot_or_argument: Yorick sets out alone, unprovided, and falls into a succession of small encounters - the monk of Calais, the fair grisette, the imprisoned French volunteer, the orphan girl at the convent gate, the dying lover at Lyons. Each meeting asks of him a feeling he is not always equal to, and his own vanity and desire are reported with the same candour as his tenderness. The journey ends with the lady of the last part unpossessed, the traveller's resolutions defeated and renewed.
narrative_structure: A loose first-person journal of episodes without continuous plot, arranged in short titled sequences; the movement is emotional rather than geographical, and the reader supplies the connections.
principal_characters: Mr. Yorick; the monk of Calais; the poor grisette; Maria, the orphan at the convent; the captive of the war and the company of the road
literary_form: sentimental travel narrative in prose
meter_and_prosody: An interrupted, breathless prose of half-sentences, dashes and exclamations, with the apostrophe to the heart as its characteristic cadence.
historical_context: Published in 1768 after the author's continental tour of the previous years and the death of his father, in the season of the cult of feeling, the sensibility controversy and the Anglo-French travel of the peace; it was answered at once by a rival's travels.
literary_significance: It is the defining text of literary sentimentalism and one of the most imitated prose styles of the century, and its treatment of sympathy as a precarious, sexual and self-interested feeling shaped the later novel of feeling.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the persona of the sermons retained.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1768 in two volumes in duodecimo, with a second edition in the same year; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition.

title: The Castle of Otranto
alternative_titles: The Castle of Otranto. A Story. Translated by William Marshal, Gent. From the Original Italian of Onuphrio Murelli
description: A Gothic tale of a tyrant prince of Apulia, his giant helmet, his murdered son and the prophecy that his castle and name would fall to the rightful possessor, published as a translation from an Italian original of the sixteenth century. It founded the romance of terror and supplied the machinery, the castle and the curse that the following generation of writers inherited.
plot_or_argument: Manfred's son Conrad is crushed to death by an enormous helmet on the day of his marriage, and Manfred, needing an heir, designs to divorce his wife and take the young Isabella himself. Isabella flees through the castle's secret passages, and the captive Theodore is discovered and released, Manfred's daughter Matilda being killed by her father's mistake in the dark. The prophecy is fulfilled as the castle falls and the true possession is restored to Theodore, Manfred retiring to a cloister.
narrative_structure: A short continuous romance in five acts or chapters of the drama-like design, with the supernatural machinery appearing at the decisive moments; the second edition added the author's own preface and defence of romance.
principal_characters: Manfred; Hippolita his wife; Matilda his daughter; Conrad and the murdered line; Isabella the escaped bride; Theodore the captive; the hermits and Friar Jerome
literary_form: Gothic romance and tale of terror
meter_and_prosody: A rapid, dramatic prose of portent and exclamation, modelled on the phraseology of the old translation and the tragedy of the stage; the inserted supernatural actions are reported in a plain chronicle manner.
historical_context: Written at Strawberry Hill amid the antiquarian revival and published in 1764, in the season of the debate over the licentiousness of fiction and of the quarrel over the authenticity of the old romances; the second edition's confessions of the trick answered the charge of forgery.
literary_significance: It is the founding work of the Gothic and the origin of a whole century's popular fiction; its prefatory theory of romance made it also a piece of criticism, and its imitation of the old tales defined the literature of terror.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published as a translation and a reprint from an unseen Italian original, a device withdrawn in the second edition, which acknowledged the modern authorship.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1764 in duodecimo with the translator's title-page, the second edition in 1765 adding the author's preface; the text is often read with the critical defence by a fellow writer on romance.

title: The Mysterious Mother
description: A closet tragedy of a mother's incestuous passion for her son, written for private performance and printed at the author's villa press. It is the most daring of the century's domestic horrors and an experiment in placing an unrepresentable subject at the centre of a regular tragedy.
plot_or_argument: The Countess of Ardenal, whose husband has died and whose son has been kept from her, conceives an unlawful and secret passion for the young count himself. She intercepts his marriage, imprisons his beloved and pursues him with designs that her attendants misread as tenderness. The discoveries arrive too late, the young count learns the truth and kills himself, and the countess's guilt is exposed to the house in a catastrophe of horror rather than of pity.
narrative_structure: A regular five-act tragedy of secrets and delayed discovery, with the mother's soliloquies carrying the horror and the final recognition producing the catastrophe; written to be read and privately acted rather than staged.
principal_characters: the Countess of Ardenal; the young Count her son; his betrothed and her friends; the attendants and officers of the house
literary_form: tragedy in five acts, a closet and private-press drama
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a deliberately old-fashioned and sometimes uneven regularity, with a strong use of the sententious pause and the ominous half-revealed phrase.
historical_context: Printed at the villa printing press in 1768 after the author's retirement from active politics, in the season of the domestic tragedy and of the analysis of horror in fiction; its subject was one the public stage could not have carried.
literary_significance: It is the century's most extreme attempt to write the unspeakable family passion as tragedy and a key document of the transmission of Gothic horror from romance into drama.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; printed privately at the author's press with his name withdrawn but never in doubt among his circle.
bibliographical_notes: Printed at the villa press in 1768 in a small edition in octavo or quarto, followed by a London issue in the collected editions; the standard text is that of the private print with its prefatorial argument.

title: Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third
alternative_titles: Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third
Doubts on the History of Richard III
description: A controversial historical argument that the standard history of Richard III is a fabrication of the victorious house, the evidence being examined point by point against the chroniclers. It is an early and influential piece of critical historical method, and its defence of the king's reputation provoked a long pamphlet war.
plot_or_argument: The work reviews the charges against Richard - the murder of the princes, the death of his wife, the tyranny and the usurpation - and finds in each case either no contemporary evidence or evidence contradicting the received story. It argues that the chronicles were composed under the new dynasty and that the most damning particulars were invented after the event. The conclusion leaves the king's guilt undemonstrated and his character to be reformed by the reader.
narrative_structure: A dissertation in numbered particulars, each charge stated, its authorities compared and its improbability urged; the argument is juridical and accumulative rather than narrative.
principal_characters: King Richard the Third; the princes in the Tower; the chroniclers and their patrons; the historians of the Tudor age
literary_form: historical dissertation and critical enquiry
meter_and_prosody: A cool, ironical and closely reasoned prose of the case and the query, with the rhetorical understatement used as a weapon against authority.
historical_context: Published in 1768 in the season of the antiquarian revival and of the new criticism of the chronicles, and answered by several hostile pieces before the century's end; its composition coincided with the author's own historical and edition work.
literary_significance: It founded the modern defence tradition of Richard's reign and is a landmark in the application of evidential scepticism to English history, anticipating the source criticism of the following century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at first and acknowledged by the author, the dispute with the answerers being documented in his letters.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1768 in a small octavo or quarto with the reprint of a preceding tract, and reissued in the collected historical work; the standard text follows the first issue.

title: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole
alternative_titles: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole at Strawberry Hill
description: A room-by-room account of the author's Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill, its collections, its chapels and its libraries, written for the guidance of visitors and printed at his own instance. It is the founding document of the Gothic revival house as a literary and antiquarian artefact.
plot_or_argument: The description leads the visitor through the exterior and the several apartments, reporting the arrangements of the Gothic chambers, the painted glass, the armour, the books and the relics with their provenances. It explains the taste and the scholarship that assembled them, and defends the villa's imitations of the old styles as faithful and instructive. The account of the collection ends with the library and the collections of prints and drawings, the whole forming a theory of antiquarian pleasure.
narrative_structure: A topographical and inventory description ordered by the plan of the house, with inserted catalogues and historical notes on individual pieces; there is no argument beyond the tour.
literary_form: antiquarian description and catalogue of a collection
meter_and_prosody: A plain descriptive prose of measurement, provenance and modest comment, with the epigraphic and heraldic phrases of the antiquarian tradition.
historical_context: Printed in 1784 in the season of the vogue for Strawberry Hill and of the author's late quarrels over the authenticity of the relics he displayed; the villa itself, built and altered over some thirty years, is the work the book describes.
literary_significance: It established the model of the described Gothic house and is the primary source for the taste, the antiquarian methods and the humour of the century's most famous literary residence.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work was printed by the owner's direction, and the later editions were enlarged by other hands after his death.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1784 in a small privately circulated edition in octavo, with enlarged issues following in the 1790s; the standard reference is to the first issue with the later additions noted.

title: The Old English Baron
alternative_titles: The Old English Baron: A Gothic Story
description: A Gothic romance written deliberately as a correction of the excesses of the first tale of terror, in which the supernatural is reduced to a single decent apparition and the passions are kept within probability. It first appeared under another title and was reissued and long known as the story of the old English baron.
plot_or_argument: The infant heir of a castle is put out of his inheritance by a usurping steward, and is fostered in ignorance of his rank by the very family that dispossessed him. He grows up generous and in love with the daughter of the house, while the ghost of his father appears at a banquet to repeat the injuries of the past. The discovery of his birth restores the estate, the fraud of the steward is punished, and the claim of the lovers is allowed.
narrative_structure: A short continuous romance in the manner of the old tale, with the apparition placed at the structural centre and the recognition supplying the close; the sequence is restrained and single-threaded.
principal_characters: the dispossessed young heir; the foster-family of the castle; the daughter he loves; the usurping steward of the estate; the ghost of the former lord
literary_form: Gothic romance and tale of probability
meter_and_prosody: An even, unornamented prose imitating the manner of the old English tales, with the supernatural scenes reported in short and grave sentences.
historical_context: Written in the late 1770s in the wake of the first Gothic novel and of the controversy over its machinery, and published in a sequence of issues between 1777 and 1778; its preface and its practice form a deliberate critical answer to its model.
literary_significance: It was the most successful Gothic tale of the 1770s and 1780s and the standard example of the rational reformed romance, and its theory of probability influenced the definition of the Gothic throughout the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at the first issue and with the author's name in the later editions and in the critical history she afterwards wrote.
bibliographical_notes: First issued in 1777 in a small octavo under an alternative title and reissued as the old English baron in 1778, with many reprints through the 1780s and 1790s, often as a companion to the tale it answered.

title: The Progress of Romance
alternative_titles: The Progress of Romance, through various Ages; consisting of a Historical and Critical Account of the Most Popular Writers of that Famous Class of Composition
description: A critical and historical account of the prose romance from the Greek and the Eastern tales through the chivalry of the Middle Ages to the writer's own day, delivered in two volumes of survey and judgment. It is one of the first sustained histories of prose fiction in English and a defence of romance on rational grounds.
plot_or_argument: The work traces the rise and declension of the romantic tale, examining its Eastern and Greek originals, the Arabian and Spanish collections, and the chivalric romances of the Middle Ages. It passes to the pastoral and heroic romance of France and to the modern novel, weighing the beauties and the improbabilities of each. Its conclusion defends the regulated use of the marvellous and judges the present taste by the standard of the old tales.
narrative_structure: A chronological critical history in two volumes, arranged by schools and periods with abstracts and quotations of the examples and with the reviewer's judgments throughout.
literary_form: critical history and dissertation on prose fiction
meter_and_prosody: A clear and moderate critical prose of estimate and comparison, with the quoted translations used as evidence of manner.
historical_context: Published in 1785 after the author's own practice in Gothic and sentimental romance, in the season of the quarrel over the novel's morality and of the first attempts at a history of English fiction.
literary_significance: It is a foundational text of the scholarly history of the novel and of the eighteenth century's attempt to classify romance, and it gives the period's most articulate defence of the tale of imagination.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and related by her to her own fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1785 in two volumes in octavo, with the second volume containing the later periods; no modern complete edition is standard and the work is cited from the first issue.

title: Vathek
alternative_titles: The History of the Caliph Vathek
description: An Arabian tale of a curious and voluptuous caliph who pursues knowledge and power until he is carried down into the palace of Eblis. It was composed in French by its author and issued in English in 1786, and its magnificence of description and its philosophy of despair made it at once notorious and influential.
plot_or_argument: Vathek, caliph of Samarah, abandons the duties and the pleasures of his throne for the search after intellectual power, and is tempted by a sorcerer's project of an underground palace. He abandons the worship of his fathers for the star-worship of his cousin Carathis, and with her and the genii penetrates the cavernous halls of Eblis. He is sealed there in the company of the Petrified Worshippers of the Stars, doomed to an eternity of unsatisfied desire, while the tale reports his former splendour and his mother's prophecy.
narrative_structure: A single continuous oriental tale with the frame of prophecy and the descent as its climax, arranged as a sequence of spectacular tableaux; the interpolated stories of the palace of Eblis are set within the last movement.
principal_characters: Vathek the caliph of Samarah; Carathis his cousin and temptress; the old sorcerer Holgher; the rebellious genii and the prince of the palace of Eblis; the mother and the prophetess of the opening
literary_form: oriental tale and philosophical romance
meter_and_prosody: A prose of superb and accumulated description, translated and revised from the author's French, with the long period of the catalogue and the terrible closure of the sentence as its characteristic effects.
historical_context: Composed in French during the author's villa years in the early 1780s and published in English translation in 1786, with the French original printed soon afterwards; it stands in the line of the Arabian tales and of the Gothic romance of the same decade.
literary_significance: It is the most splendid of the century's literary arabesques and a central text of the Gothic-Oriental imagination, its palace of Eblis being one of the great visions of despair in English prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution of the design uncontested, the English first edition being a translation from the author's French manuscript made with his knowledge and revised by him, the translator's share being traditionally assigned to a scholar of the day; the record is here held under the author's name alone.
bibliographical_notes: First published in English in London in 1786 in a volume issued with other tales, the French text following in the later 1780s; the composition dates are not asserted here, the usual account placing them in the author's early twenties.

title: The Rivals
description: A comedy of Irish and London gallantry, of fathers' authority and of the mistakes of young lovers, its fame resting on its dialogue, its first act's declaration of war against sentiment on the stage and its creation of the century's most quoted blundering matron.
plot_or_argument: Ferdinand Absolute, reported dead by a feigned letter, is loved in absence by his betrothed, while his father returns from Ireland to marry a young wife and to dispose of the lovers. Julia elopes by mistake with the wrong lover, Lydia Languish is courted by an assumed name, and the Irish captain Sir Lucius is challenged over a letter he does not understand. The several mistakes are cleared at the end, the fathers consent, and the double marriage is prepared.
narrative_structure: Five-act comedy of erring letters and mistaken persons, with the famous prefacial ploy of the author answering his first-night critics; the plot turns on a chain of written and reported misunderstandings.
principal_characters: Mrs. Malaprop; Sir Anthony Absolute; Captain Absolute; Faulkland; Julia; Lydia Languish; Sir Lucius O'Trigger; Fag and the servants
literary_form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Brisk prose dialogue of repartee and malapropism, with the sentimental and the high-flown styles deliberately deflated; the letters and messages read aloud are the comic set pieces.
historical_context: First performed at Covent Garden in January 1775, in the season of the quarrel between sentimental and laughing comedy, and of the Irish comedy of the London stage; its author was a young playwright soon to be a theatre manager.
literary_significance: It restored the comedy of humour and intrigue to the London stage after the sentimental fashion and remains a standing repertory piece; its prefatory attack on sentiment on the stage is a document of the century's genre quarrel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the success of the revivals following an uncertain first night.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1775 in octavo following the second season's success, with the preface and the epilogues included; standard texts follow the first edition with the early acting versions noted.

title: The Duenna
description: A comic opera in three acts, founded on the old Spanish play of the duenna and carried by a score of popular songs, and one of the most successful musical entertainments of the century. It was the joint work of a young playwright and of the composer with whom he was connected by family, and its first run outdid the fashion of the ballad opera.
plot_or_argument: Two lovers are kept apart by a jealous father and his duenna, the elderly Don D. being made to marry the lady's duenna in his own mistake. Isaac the rich Jew is cozened out of his intended bride, and the elopements, disguises and forged letters clear themselves in the last act. The songs interrupt and advance the intrigue, and the comedy ends with the double marriage and the duenna's confusion.
narrative_structure: Three-act comic opera of spoken dialogue and set songs, the plot a regular intrigue of mistake with the musical numbers functioning as the sentimental set pieces.
principal_characters: the duenna Donna Rodriguez; the jealous father Don Jerome; Clara his daughter; Isaac Mendosa; Antonio and the lover of the elopement
literary_form: comic opera with spoken dialogue
meter_and_prosody: Prose dialogue in the ballad-opera manner, with songs in the common lyric measures of the stage, several of them still sung as independent airs.
historical_context: First performed at Covent Garden in November 1775, in the season of the quarrel over the relative merits of opera and comedy and of the manager's own struggles to revive English musical drama; its authorship was debated in the press at the time of its first run.
literary_significance: It is the most durable English comic opera before the nineteenth century and a decisive step in the revival of musical theatre in London, its songs remaining in the repertory longer than the play.
attribution_notes: Collaborative: the spoken dialogue and the general design are assigned to the playwright, and the composition to Thomas Linley, whose share was publicly questioned in 1775 and whose family connection with the author complicates the record; only the playwright is named in the relationship map.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1775 in octavo with the musical selections separately issued, and reprinted in the collected plays of the author; the standard text follows the first edition with the songs as performed.

title: The School for Scandal
alternative_titles: The School for Scandal: A Comedy
description: The greatest comedy of the late eighteenth century, a play about scandal-mongering and hypocritical virtue in which the surface candour of a fashionable society is dissected by a series of eavesdroppings. Its famous fourth-act screen scene gathers the whole design into one tableau.
plot_or_argument: A house of professed candour is divided against itself: the outwardly moral younger brother supplants his frank and spendthrift elder, and a circle of wits live on the malice of the tea-table. Sir Peter Teazle, newly married to a country girl, is set against his wife by the same tribe, and the wife is taught the ways of the town. The discovery of the hypocrite by the try-all brother and the exposure of the school of scandal in the screen scene restore the elder brother and reform the young couple.
narrative_structure: Five-act comedy of intrigue and discovery, its turns effected by concealed hearing and the misreport of conversation; the dialogue advances the plot almost entirely by what is overheard.
principal_characters: Sir Peter Teazle; Lady Teazle; Joseph Surface; Charles Surface; Sir Oliver Surface; Lady Sneerwell; Snake; Maria; the backbiters of the breakfast table
literary_form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: A brilliant prose dialogue of epigram, retort and malaprop-free precision, the high style of the moral sententiae being reserved for parody; the speeches are built to be quoted.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in May 1777 after the failure of a rival play on the same design, in the season in which its author became a principal manager of the house; the comedy of sensibility and the comedy of laughter were then openly contending for the stage.
literary_significance: It is the final masterpiece of the English comedy of manners and the standard instance of the argument that society's conversation is a form of action; it has never left the repertory.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and recorded in the manager's own accounts of the season.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1777 in octavo following the first run, with the early acting editions altering some lines; the standard text follows the first edition with the variant readings noted.

title: The Critic
description: A comic rehearsal piece, subtitled a tragedy in the irony of the day, in which the pretences of contemporary tragedy and criticism are exposed by the staging of an absurdly grandiose play within the play. It was the last great success of the eighteenth-century theatre of self-reference.
plot_or_argument: A family of country gentlefolk and their hangers-on go to see a new tragedy, and the business of the pit, the boxes and the green-room is reported before and after the performance. The play itself, a monstrous romance of terror with an old castle and a ghost, is rehearsed and criticised by its authors and by the wits of the town. The exposure of the bombast ends the comedy, the lovers of the frame being united in the last scene.
narrative_structure: Two-act comedy of the rehearsal and the audience, with a running performance of the inserted tragedy; the frame and the inserted piece comment on each other throughout.
principal_characters: Mr. Puff, the author of the inserted tragedy; his friends the critics and the observers of the pit; the family of the frame and the lovers of the underplot; the players of the burlesque romance
literary_form: comic rehearsal drama with inserted burlesque tragedy
meter_and_prosody: Prose dialogue for the comedy and an exaggerated blank verse and declamation for the inserted tragedy, the joke lying in the contrast of the two registers.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1781, in the season of the manager's quarrels, the revival of old plays and the persistent debate about tragic declamation; its target includes the contemporary school of domestic terror on the stage.
literary_significance: It is the century's sharpest analysis of theatrical taste and of the critic's trade, and its portrait of the self-satisfied dramatist remains the stock image of literary vanity.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested, though the author's share was discussed in the press in relation to an earlier fragment of the same design; published in his name.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1781 in octavo after the first run, with the epilogue and the songs; standard editions follow the first edition with the acting versions noted.

title: Douglas
description: A Scottish tragedy of hidden birth, maternal love and fatal revenge, written by a minister of the Kirk and first seen in private performance at Edinburgh before its London production. It was the most celebrated and most attacked new tragedy of the mid-century, and its pathos was held to have regenerated the national stage.
plot_or_argument: Douglas, a youth of unknown parentage nurtured in the house of Lady Randolph, loves her ward and is beloved in return, while the Dane Norval presses his suit upon the lady. Norval is discovered to be the destroyer of Randolph, the lady's first husband, and Douglas kills him in the revenge he does not understand. The recognition of Douglas as the lady's long-lost son comes too late, and he dies in her arms after the fatal discovery.
narrative_structure: Five-act regular tragedy of recognition and revenge, the delay of the discovery providing the suspense and the closing recognition the catastrophe; the language is deliberately simple and grave.
principal_characters: Douglas; Lady Randolph; Norval the Dane; the ward who loves Douglas; the attendants and retainers of the Scottish house
literary_form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Plain and elevated blank verse of the school of the older English tragedy, with the short sententious line and the apostrophes of maternal grief as its characteristic effects.
historical_context: Seen privately at Edinburgh in 1756 and first played in London at Covent Garden in April 1757, in the season of the debate over the stage's morality and of the new Scottish literary confidence; its clerical author was attacked from the pulpit and defended in the press.
literary_significance: It established the model of the highland and national tragedy for the following generation, was the vehicle of the age's most admired acting, and carried the argument about the theatre's moral authority into Scotland.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in the accounts of the first London performance.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1757 in octavo with the dedication and the remarks on the performance, and reissued with the author's collected writings; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: The Gamester
description: A domestic tragedy of a gentleman undone by the gaming table, whose weakness is exploited by those about him until he destroys his family and himself. It was one of the most effective and most imitated of the century's moral tragedies and remained a stock piece of the repertory.
plot_or_argument: Beverley, an honest man with a passion for play, is drawn on by a cheating companion and by the artifices of a serving man who wins his own ends by the ruin. His wife's remonstrances and the losses at the table drive him to despair, and he is led by a false report of her infidelity to a fatal act. The discovery of the cheat and of the innocent wife comes too late, and Beverley dies penitent on a bed of straw in the playhouse's most quoted scene of domestic ruin.
narrative_structure: Five-act regular domestic tragedy, the action contracted about the game and the house, with the villainy of the inferiors supplying the machinery of the fall; the catastrophe is a death-bed discovery.
principal_characters: Beverley the gamester; his wife; the designing servant; the cheating friend at the table; the family and the creditors of the ruin
literary_form: domestic and sentimental tragedy in five acts
meter_and_prosody: A grave and affective blank verse of the middle style, with the homely sentences of the domestic scenes and the long dying periods of the last act.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1753, in the season of the new statutes against gaming and of the vogue for moral domestic tragedy; the writer was a periodical essayist and editor of the same years.
literary_significance: It is the most successful of the eighteenth-century plays on the ruinous passions of the middle class and a central text of the sentimental theatre, its ending being a byword for the pathos of the domestic catastrophe.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with a dedication that argues the moral design.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1753 in octavo after the first run, with frequent reissues and revivals through the century; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: False Delicacy
description: A sentimental comedy of a young woman who loses the man she loves by an over-scrupulous reserve, written to prove that virtue itself may err by excess of refinement. It was the successful rival of a kindred play of the same season and took the argument for sentimental reformation of the stage.
plot_or_argument: A lady of exalted principles conceals her affection from the lover she has promised, from a false notion of modesty, and by her silence gives his family the opening for another match. A second pair, less refined and more frank, carry the underplot of honest inclination, and the friends and guardians divide the counsel of the world. The exposure of the mistake restores the first lovers, the comedy closing on the argument that a delicacy which costs a woman her happiness is false.
narrative_structure: Five-act comedy of concealed feeling and mistaken counsel, with the underplot of the frank pair set against the main plot of scruple; the moral case is argued directly in the dialogue.
principal_characters: the lady of the false delicacy of the title; the lover lost by her reserve; the guardian and the friends who misadvise; the frank pair of the underplot
literary_form: sentimental comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: A smooth prose dialogue of delicate refinement and sententious argument, the emotional moments raised into short declamations of principle.
historical_context: First performed at Covent Garden in January 1766 in the same season and on the same bill as the rival comedy of the same quarrel, the contest being made the occasion of a public debate on the laughing and the sentimental comedy by the authors of both sides.
literary_significance: It is the standard example of the sentimental comedy in its hour of triumph, and the season's pamphlets on the two species of comedy make it a fixed point in the history of the century's genre quarrel.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the prefatory argument on the design.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1766 in octavo following the run, with the prefatory matter of the season's dispute; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: The Belle's Stratagem
description: The most successful comedy by a woman dramatist of the late eighteenth century, in which a young woman determined to be won rather than to win pursues the man she loves through a series of disguises. Its heroine's stratagems make it the most direct descendant on the stage of the amatory fiction of the earlier century.
plot_or_argument: Letitia Hardy, promised to a young man of fortune who does not know her worth, resolves to make him pursue her by assuming a different woman each night, first as a neighbour's daughter and then in other persons of the town. Her friend and the gallants of her father's circle are drawn into the design, and the lovers' fathers make their own plans of marriage. The last stratagem brings the lover to a declaration, and the discoveries justify the heroine's conduct and complete the match.
narrative_structure: Five-act comedy of personation, the successive disguises supplying the movement and the final recognition the close; the heroine's management of the plot is the play's governing interest.
principal_characters: Letitia Hardy; Dorilton, the lover she must win; her friend of the stratagems; the fathers who arrange the matches; the gallants and the imposed-with company
literary_form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: A bright prose dialogue of retort and affected persons, with the disguised speeches carrying the satire of fashionable address; the songs and letters serve as set pieces.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1780, in the season in which the woman dramatist became a regular attraction of the theatres and in which the old device of personation was revived for a polite audience.
