literary_significance: It holds the place of the century's most durable comedy by a woman playwright and is a key text for the history of the female plotter in drama and of the theatrical revival of romantic disguise.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after her first successes, though some of her verse had circulated earlier under a poetic signature.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1780 in octavo after the first run, with frequent revivals and reprints; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: Evelina; or, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World
alternative_titles: Evelina, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World
description: The history of a young woman of unknown birth introduced by her guardian's family into London and Bristol society, told in her letters home to the grandfather she has never known. Its publication was anonymous and its immediate success surprised its author, who had thrown it out as a juvenile exercise.
plot_or_argument: Evelina Anville, the daughter of a private and disobliged marriage, is taken by her grandfather Lady Howard's connection into the company of the Mirvan family. She is annoyed by Madame Duval, her mother's relation, insulted and compromised in the gardens and at the assemblies, and carried through the theatre, the balls and the rackets of the town. At Bristol she is robbed and rescued, and in London her conduct under continual provocation is vindicated; the discovery of her birth and her grandfather's consent prepare the marriage with the man she has deserved.
narrative_structure: A novel in a series of letters, principally from Evelina to Mr. Villars, with the letters of others supplying the report of her conduct; the sequence of public amusements forms the social anatomy of the book.
principal_characters: Evelina Anville; Mr. Villars; Lady Howard; Mrs. and Miss Mirvan; Captain Mirvan; Madame Duval; Lord Ormont; the servants and the assistants of the town
literary_form: epistolary novel of manners
meter_and_prosody: A carefully graded epistolary prose, the heroine's letters polite, naive and increasingly articulate, the comic letters of Captain Mirvan and of Madame Duval carrying the broad humour; the style of the reporting letters is the book's chief instrument.
historical_context: Published in London in 1778 by a young woman writing from the household of the musical family of the Drury Lane manager, in the season of the new attention to the manners of the town, the assemblies and the public gardens, and of the quarrel over women's novels.
literary_significance: It created the comedy-of-manners novel written by a woman and is the standard account of the initiation of a girl into the sexual and social grammar of polite London; its influence on the later novel of observation is very large.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; issued anonymously as by a lady in the first edition, its authorship being declared by the writer in the second and later editions and established by her papers.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1778 in two volumes in duodecimo without the author's name, with a fourth edition in the following year carrying her acknowledgement; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition.

title: Cecilia; or, Memoirs of an Heiress
description: The history of an heiress whose fortune makes her the property of everyone who desires it, and who is worn between the claims of several marriages and the demands of a society that cannot conceive of a woman with money acting for herself. It is the broadest and most public of the author's novels, ending in a catastrophe the century's readers thought severe.
plot_or_argument: Cecilia Beverley, left an estate on condition that her husband take the name, is courted by a lawyer of merit and by a young fellow of fashion, while her guardians consult their own interest in the choice. She is carried to Bristol and into the companies of the town, is drawn into a friend's distress and loses money at the card table through the artifice of a designing relation. She at last accepts the suit of the man she had undervalued, and his death from a wound received in defence of her reputation exposes the world that destroyed him. The novel closes on her renunciation of society and her retirement, the heiress having purchased her independence at the price of every attachment.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration in five or six volumes, with the heroine's consciousness reported rather than voiced, and a public plot of debts, assemblies and the law; the conclusion is a retirement rather than a marriage.
principal_characters: Cecilia Beverley; Mr. Belfield; the young man of fashion; her guardians and their families; Madame de Burgh; the friends of the town and of Bristol
literary_form: novel of manners and of the marriage market
meter_and_prosody: An ample, reflective third-person prose with the free indirect report of the heroine's opinion, and the epistolary and conversational set pieces of the earlier novel retained in modified form.
historical_context: Published by subscription in 1782, in the season of the debates on women's property, the law of marriage and the influence of the fashionable circle; its author was by then a recognised novelist and a member of the Bluestocking society.
literary_significance: It is the most complete analysis of the position of the propertied woman in the fiction of the century before the age of its author's rivals, and its argument about independence shaped the later novel of women's circumstance.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the anonymous first novel, the issue by subscription being recorded in its own lists.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1782 in five volumes in duodecimo by subscription, with a second edition soon after; the standard scholarly edition follows the first.

title: The Witlings
description: A five-act comedy of the blue-stockings and the tea-table wits of the town, written for the stage but never performed in the author's lifetime, its rehearsal being stopped by the interference of her father and of the leading players. It survives in manuscript and in modern print as the sharpest contemporary attack on the society of wit.
plot_or_argument: A young lady of the school of the witlings is set by her friends against the plain suitor her family approves, while the club of the blue-stockings, its critics and its authors, divides the conversation of the town between pretension and malice. The several devices of the wits, the verses and the reviews, expose the vanity of the set. The comedy was withdrawn before performance, and its argument about the price of literary reputation was left to be read.
narrative_structure: A regular five-act comedy of conversation and pretension, the satire concentrated in the scenes of the blue-stocking circle; the text is that of the withdrawn manuscript.
principal_characters: the young lady of the witlings; her mother and the friends of the circle; the plain suitor disapproved by the set; the critics and the authors of the tea-table club
literary_form: comedy in five acts, unperformed
meter_and_prosody: A brilliant conversational prose of quotation, review and affected sensibility, the jargon of the witlings being reproduced for exposure.
historical_context: Written in 1779 in the season of the quarrel between the author's father and the theatres, and suppressed at the rehearsal stage with the intervention of the leading manager; the Bluestocking society and the review trade supplied its immediate targets.
literary_significance: It is a primary document of the century's argument about women's literary sociability and of the practical censorship of the stage, and its suppression has become a central case in the history of women's access to publication.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the comedy remained in manuscript and in the author's papers, and was not printed until modern times, so that no first edition date is asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Composed in 1779 and never published in the author's lifetime; first printed in the twentieth century from the manuscript, and included in the modern collected early comedies; the date of composition is recorded and that of publication left null.

title: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
alternative_titles: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, in the Early Part of Life
Thoughts on the Education of Daughters. In the Early Part of Life; with Remarks on the Management of Children, from Birth to the Age of Ten Years
description: A conduct and educational treatise for the management of girls from earliest childhood, drawn from the author's experience as a governess and a schoolmistress. It argues for the cultivation of reason, truthfulness and independence in girls, and for the reform of the needlework and accomplishments curriculum of the day.
plot_or_argument: The work sets out the duties of the mother and the governess in the first years of a girl's life, treating the government of the temper, the formation of habits of veracity and the dangers of false modesty. It criticises the female academies and their round of accomplishments, recommends the study of religion and of reason, and gives directions on health, amusement and the choice of company. Its conclusion is that a woman's virtue depends on her understanding being taught to act for itself.
narrative_structure: A continuous didactic essay in numbered heads and reflections, with the instance and the practical direction alternating; the argument is orderly rather than systematic.
literary_form: conduct and educational treatise in prose
meter_and_prosody: A clear, earnest and direct prose of instruction, with the occasional apostrophe to mothers and the sententious summation of the section.
historical_context: Published in 1787 after the author's keeping of a school for girls and her service as a governess, in the season of the public debate on female academies and on women's rational education, the same debate that occupied the Bluestocking writers of the day.
literary_significance: It is the first published work of the century's most influential advocate of women's rational education and supplies the practical ground of the later argument about the rights and the cultivation of women's minds.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was issued without the writer's name in the first edition, its authorship being established by her correspondence and by the later issues.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1787 in a small octavo or duodecimo volume, with an American issue in the same year; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: Mary: A Fiction
description: The first novel of a writer then unknown to the reading public, the history of a young woman of ardent imagination and sensibility, married without affection and ruined by the loss of those she loves. It is the most openly romantic of its author's works and a deliberate exposure of the education of feeling.
plot_or_argument: Mary, the daughter of an affectation of religion and a mother of sensibility, is educated in romance and forms attachments of extravagant intensity, first to a schoolfellow and then to a friend of her childhood. Her father's convenience marries her to a man she does not love, and the births and deaths of her children, the failure of her friends and her own wandering complete the trial. She ends in a state of grief and religious doubt, her sensibility having been given her as a substitute for an education of the mind.
narrative_structure: Third-person narration of a single life in short chapters, organised as the history of an education in feeling; the episodes are sequenced by attachment and loss rather than by intrigue.
principal_characters: Mary; her mother and father; the friend of her childhood; the husband of her parents' convenience; her children
literary_form: novel; fiction of sensibility and female education
meter_and_prosody: An impassioned and exclamatory prose of the culture of feeling, with the abstract noun of sensibility carrying much of the argument; the sentences rise to the apostrophe and the apostasy.
historical_context: Published in 1788, in the season of the novel of sensibility's crisis and of the author's own first engagements with the publishers and the philosophical circle, its design answering the conduct literature she had recently written.
literary_significance: It is the founding fiction of its author's career and a key text for the analysis of sensibility as a female education, anticipating the later argument about the reason and the situation of women.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously with a prefatory advertisement, its authorship established by the publisher's records and by the later issues.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1788 in a small octavo volume, reprinted in the collected works of the following years; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: The Adventures of Gil Blas of Santillane
alternative_titles: The History and Adventures of the Famous Gil Blas of Santillane
description: A translation of the Spanish picaresque romance of Le Sage, issued in several volumes and carrying the career of a servant of great part from the roads of Spain to the courts of the dukes and the practice of physic. It became the standard English Gil Blas and a school for the translators of the following generation.
plot_or_argument: Gil Blas, a boy of Astorga, runs from his uncles and falls into the company of robbers, from whom he escapes to service in the great houses of Madrid. He passes through the keeping of an archbishop, a nobleman and a physician, is enriched and ruined by his own knaveries and by the examples of his masters, and at last marries and retires to tell his history. The sequence of services forms a continuous satire on the professions and the vanity of the world.
narrative_structure: First-person picaresque autobiography in books, the episodes arranged as successive services and recoveries, with the inserted tales of the patrons carrying the satire.
principal_characters: Gil Blas of Santillane; his uncles and the robbers of the road; the successive masters of his service in Madrid; the physicians and the ministers of the interpolated tales; the housekeeper and the wife
literary_form: translation of a picaresque romance; prose fiction in books
meter_and_prosody: A robust and idiomatic English prose rendering of the French original, its sentences adapted to the colloquial energy of the picaresque manner.
historical_context: Published in London in 1749 in the season of the great translation enterprises of the hack and the aspirant, the original French having been composed by Le Sage from Spanish materials, and the English market having already tried partial versions.
literary_significance: It gave English readers their habitual Gil Blas and was a principal channel through which the Spanish picaresque reached the mid-century novelists, the translator's own fiction owing something to its method.
attribution_notes: The translation is uncontroversially the work of the novelist here recorded, though it drew on and superseded earlier English versions; the French original is the work of another hand.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1749 in four volumes in duodecimo or octavo, with revised and reprinted issues later in the century; the dates of the several volumes are not separately asserted here.

title: Original Stories from Real Life
alternative_titles: Original Stories from Real Life. With Reflections, Calculated to the Early Formation of the Mind on Principles of Truth and Benevolence
description: A book of tales for children, framed as the instruction given by a governess to two girls, each story being worked up into a reflection on truth, benevolence, industry and justice. Its first edition was designed and engraved by an artist then young, and its rational morality marks a stage in the history of children's reading.
plot_or_argument: The governess of the household leads her little charges through the observation of the world about them - the poor, the animal creation, the labouring family, the proud and the falsehood-teller - and out of each case draws a lesson of duty. The children's own questions and faults carry the narrative, and the stories of the people they meet supply the illustration. The book closes on the principle that the imagination of a child must be governed by reason and by sympathy with the suffering.
narrative_structure: A framed sequence of short didactic tales and conversations, the frame of the governess's instruction supplying the reflection and the inset stories the example; each number ends with an application.
principal_characters: the governess who instructs; the two girls of her charge; the poor families and the servants of the inset tales; the animals and the objects of the children's curiosity
literary_form: children's didactic fiction in framed tales
meter_and_prosody: A clear and argumentative prose of conversation adapted to juvenile readers, with the reflective summing-up in a sententious cadence.
historical_context: Published in 1788 after the author's first work on female education and among the new rational children's books of the period, in the circle of the dissenting publisher who also issued the scientific and educational works of the day.
literary_significance: It is an important document of the eighteenth-century education of childhood and of the moral use of sympathy, and it shows the author's pedagogy before the argument of her later works on women.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the design and plates by a fellow writer and engraver of the same circle.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1788 in a small octavo with designs, and reissued in several editions within the decade, some with altered matter; the standard scholarly text follows the first edition.

title: On the Importance of Religious Opinions
alternative_titles: On the Importance of Religious Opinions. Translated from the French of Necker
description: A translation of the French devotional and argumentative work of a statesman-writer of the preceding generation, undertaken by a young author then defining her own religious position. The version was issued with the translator's own prefatory reflection on the temper of the age.
plot_or_argument: The work argues that the opinion a man holds on religious questions is of the first consequence to his conduct and happiness, and examines the duties of the inquirer after truth. It distinguishes between the forms of belief and their effects on the heart, presses the necessity of seriousness and charity, and answers those who profess indifference. The translator's preface urges the same argument on the readers of her own country.
narrative_structure: A continuous argumentative treatise in short chapters, with the translator's prefixed discourse standing as an independent essay.
literary_form: translation of a religious argument, with prefatory essay
meter_and_prosody: A plain earnest prose of the devotional argument, its periods and divisions following the French original, the prefatory matter being in the writer's own idiom.
historical_context: Published in 1788 in the season of the author's own religious enquiry, when translations of continental devotional work were a regular part of the dissenting book trade, and when the question of religious opinion was a live matter of public argument.
literary_significance: It records the religious thinking of a writer whose later work on the mind and on women's education rests on this period of enquiry, and its preface is one of her earliest published prose statements.
attribution_notes: The translation is attributed to the writer here recorded without dispute; the original remains the work of another hand, and the prefatory discourse is her own.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1788 in a small octavo or duodecimo volume with the translator's preface; the date of the French original is not asserted here.

title: The Female Reader
alternative_titles: The Female Reader: Pieces, Prose and Verse, Selected from the Most Classick Writers and Calculated as a Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
The Female Reader. A Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
description: An anthology of prose and verse selected for the use of young women and furnished with rules of reading and with the editor's remarks on taste, elocution and the choice of books. It was planned as the practical completion of a female education and issued in several volumes.
plot_or_argument: The collection passes in order through the species of composition - description, argument, narration, the drama, the epic, lyric and the letters of history - each being illustrated by extracted specimens and preceded by directions for reading it well. Remarks on the choice of books, on the cultivation of the ear and on the danger of incorrect reading supply the connective argument. Its design is to make a woman's taste an instrument of judgement rather than of amusement.
narrative_structure: A systematic anthology in classes with the editor's dissertations and notes interposed; the order of the species governs the sequence, the extracts supplying the examples.
literary_form: anthology and critical guide to reading
meter_and_prosody: A didactic prose of rule and remark for the connecting matter, the verse extracts being given as specimens of the several measures and the prose as models of style.
historical_context: Published in 1789 in the same season as the author's work on the education of women and within the dissenting and Bluestocking projects for female improvement, the anthology genre then being a principal means of literary instruction.
literary_significance: It is an important document of the pedagogy of taste for women at the end of the century and evidence of the author's methods as a critic and teacher before her political writing.
attribution_notes: Attribution established by the publisher's records and by the correspondence of the period, the work having been issued without the name of the editor; part of the compiling labour has been associated with a sister's hand, and the record is held as partial.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1789 in two volumes in duodecimo, with reissues in the following decade; the initials on the title-page are those of the editor's disguise rather than of the writer's name.

title: The Covent-Garden Tragedy
description: A two-act burlesque tragedy in which the inhabitants of a house of accommodation talk the language of virtue, tenderness and heroic distress, and the domestic tragedy of the higher classes is inverted into the parlour of the lower. It was played at Drury Lane at the end of the author's first theatrical season.
plot_or_argument: The mistress of the house and her daughter are rivals for the affection of a young gentleman of the town, each insisting on the claims of nature and of merit. The lover is torn between gratitude and passion, the officers of the watch and the creditors press upon the family, and the high tragic style is sustained through the lowest of situations. The piece ends in a catastrophe of tenderness rather than of blood, the moral being the ridiculousness of tragic phrase.
narrative_structure: A two-act farce of tragic form, the scenes arranged as the exchanges of a regular tragedy with their dignity inverted; the parody is continuous and the plot is a thin excuse.
principal_characters: Mother Punchbowl, the mistress of the house; her daughter, the rival of the same address; Dimple, the young gentleman pursued by both; the watchmen and officers of the garden
literary_form: burlesque tragedy in two acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse and the declamatory periods of tragedy used for the lowest subjects, with the couplet sententiae of the tragic closure intact; the effect depends on the discrepancy of style and scene.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in June 1732, in the season of the author's experiments in the little theatre and of the fashionable decline of tragedy, and after the burlesque success of the Tom Thumb piece of the previous year.
literary_significance: It is one of the most sustained English parodies of the diction of tragedy and a necessary link between the theatrical burlesque of the writer's early career and the theory of the ridiculous worked out in the comic prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name in the collected dramatick works of the later thirties.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in London in 1732 in octavo following the performance, and reprinted in the collected plays; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: Sensibility
alternative_titles: Sensibility. A Poem. In Two Parts
description: A moral essay in couplets on the culture of feeling, distinguishing a true from a false sensibility and arguing that tenderness without principle is a form of self-love. It was the first considerable poem of its author and established her reputation in the fashionable literary world.
plot_or_argument: The poet examines the temper of the age, in which the refinement of feeling has been mistaken for virtue, and shows the man of sensibility pursuing his own pleasure under the colour of sympathy. Examples of the false and the real are contrasted - the suffering of the poor, the distress of friendship, the duties that a feeling heart evades. The second part passes to the consolation of religion and to the assertion that sensibility must be governed by duty and by the hope of another world.
narrative_structure: A discursive poem in two parts, opening with a complaint of the manners of the age, passing through instances and characters, and closing in an elevation of principle.
literary_form: moral essay in verse
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of the Augustan school, with the closed and balanced antithesis of the sententious line and the occasional pathetical pause.
historical_context: Published in 1773, in the height of the cult of sensibility and of the first attacks upon it, and written by a young woman of the Bath and London literary circles who was shortly to become a dramatist and a conduct writer.
literary_significance: It is one of the clearest early statements of the case against the ethics of feeling, and it announced a career that was to span the century's passage from fashionable sensibility to evangelical duty.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in her collected verse.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1773 in a small quarto or octavo, with enlarged issues in the following editions; the standard text follows the first issue with the later additions.

title: Percy
description: A domestic tragedy founded on an old English ballad and on the stories of the heroic age of the north, in which a noble seducer and the ruined wife of his dependant are brought to a discovery and a catastrophe of feeling. It held the stage for many years after its author's religious conversion took her from the theatre.
plot_or_argument: A lord of high family and little principle makes an artful attack upon the wife of an officer of his household, whose tenderness and duty expose her the more. The ruin of the family, the struggles of the injured husband and the terrors of the wife carry the action to its catastrophe. The closing scenes bring the seducer to remorse and the innocent to suffering, the play arguing that passion without virtue destroys a house.
narrative_structure: A regular tragedy in five acts of the school of sentimental domestic drama, the scenes built about the several attacks and the last discovery; the catastrophe is affective rather than violent.
literary_form: domestic and sentimental tragedy in five acts
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of the mid-century school, elevated and pathetic, with the short broken line of the distress scenes and the set speeches of remonstrance.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in 1777 with success, in the season of the vogue for the ballad-derived domestic tragedy and before the author's withdrawal from the stage; it remained in the repertory into the following century.
literary_significance: It is a notable instance of the ballad revival's contribution to serious drama and of a woman's command of the tragic repertory at Drury Lane; its later history bears on the quarrel between the stage and its author's religious principles.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published with the author's name and recorded in the theatre books of the season.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1777 in octavo after the first run, with frequent reissues and acting editions; the standard text follows the first edition.

title: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse
alternative_titles: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse. By the Author of Sensibility
description: A collection of occasional essays, tales and verses gathered from the author's papers of the previous five years and published in the same season as her first tragedy. It shows the range of her early moral and sociable writing, from the character and the familiar letter to the short tale of feeling.
plot_or_argument: The volume passes from the essay on manners and on the duties of the heart to the narrative illustrations of the same themes, the tales exhibiting the errors of a good-nature ungoverned by principle. Its verses address friends and occasions, and its closing pieces turn from the world of the tea-table to the claims of religion and of seriousness. The design throughout is to recommend an active and disciplined virtue over the passive refinement of the age.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of prose essays, inset tales and occasional verse, arranged with the longer argumentative pieces first and the shorter pieces following; no continuous plot.
literary_form: essay collection and occasional verse
meter_and_prosody: Argumentative prose of the mid-century essay for the discursive pieces, and heroic couplets and lyrical stanzas for the verse, the two being kept in the polite middle register.
historical_context: Published in 1777 in the season of the author's establishment in the London and Bath circles and of her first successes on the stage, in the same years as the quarrel between the sensibility writers and their moral critics.
literary_significance: It fixed her early reputation as a moral essayist and is the base from which her later conduct writing and her religious work were developed; several of the pieces were reprinted separately through the decade.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with the advertisement of the previous poem.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1777 in octavo, with several enlarged issues in the following years; the standard text follows the first collection.

title: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind
alternative_titles: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind, Particularly with Regard to the Conduct of the Life
Letters on the Improvement of the Mind
description: A series of letters of instruction to a young woman, on the government of the temper, the use of learning, the choice of company, religion and the conduct of the common day. It became one of the most widely read of the century's female conduct books and passed through many editions.
plot_or_argument: The correspondent is guided through the duties of the mind, the culture of the understanding, the discipline of the passions and the ordering of time and fortune. Learning is recommended for judgement rather than for show, and the dangers of sensibility, of company and of expense are weighed with practical counsel. The later letters turn to religion, to the conduct of the understanding in divine matters and to the duties of the active life.
narrative_structure: A serial of familiar letters on connected heads, the sequence moving from the culture of the mind to the conduct of the life and to religion; each letter closes with a practical direction.
literary_form: conduct and educational letters; familiar essay in epistolary form
meter_and_prosody: A clear, warm and unrhetorical epistolary prose of the middle style, with the balanced sentence of moral advice and the occasional quotation of the poets.
historical_context: Published in 1773 from the circle of the Bluestocking correspondents, whose letters on female education and taste had prepared the public for such a work, and in the season of the new attention to the academies and to women's rational improvement.
literary_significance: It is a central text of the practical education of women in the later eighteenth century and a document of the Bluestocking argument that improvement of the mind and conduct of the life are one subject.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the circulation of the letters among friends.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1773 in a small octavo or duodecimo with many reissues and American editions; the standard text follows the first issue.

title: All the Works of Epictetus
alternative_titles: All the Works of Epictetus, Which are Now Extant: Consisting of His Discourses, Collect'd by Arrian; The Enchiridion; and Chapters, Collect'd by Stobaeus
description: A complete English version of the surviving works of the Stoic teacher, made from the Greek with an historical and critical preface and with annotations explaining the philosophy and its phrases. It was the work by which a woman scholar became a European byword for Greek learning.
plot_or_argument: The translation renders the discourses reported by Arrian, the handbook and the extracts preserved by Stobaeus, giving the reader the whole of Epictetus's practical philosophy. The prefatory account explains the life, the doctrine and the value of the author, and the notes open the terms of the schools. The work presents Stoic ethics as a discipline of judgement, desire and duty, useful to Christian readers as well as to philosophers.
narrative_structure: A scholarly translation in several books with a prefatory dissertation and commentarial notes; the order follows the arrangement of the Greek discourses.
principal_characters: Epictetus; his interlocutors and reporters, Arrian and Stobaeus
literary_form: translation of a philosophical text, with preface and notes
meter_and_prosody: A plain and capable prose translation of the Greek homily and diatribe, its sentences kept close to the spoken manner of the school; the prefatory matter is in the essay style of the day.
historical_context: Published in 1758 with the encouragement and the practical support of the learned women of her acquaintance, in the season of the revival of Stoic and moral-philosophical interest and of the controversy about the study of Greek by women.
literary_significance: It is one of the great achievements of eighteenth-century women's scholarship and long remained the standard English Epictetus, its reception being a decisive argument for female classical learning.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the translator's name, the undertaking having been assisted by a borrowed Greek text and by the counsel of friends.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1758 in a handsomely issued volume with the preface and notes, and reissued in a second edition in 1774; standard readers use the later reprints of this version.

title: An Essay on the Learning and Genius of Shakespeare
description: A critical essay defending Shakespeare's learning and his genius against the neoclassical objections of the previous age, and arguing that his excellences are those of an observing moralist rather than of a regular artist. It was the most influential piece of Shakespearean criticism by an eighteenth-century woman and went through several issues in its first year.
plot_or_argument: The essay reviews the charge of ignorance and of barbarous taste, and answers it by showing the reach of Shakespeare's knowledge of nature and of mankind. It defends his violation of the rules by the higher rule of probability and of instruction, and sets his moral seriousness against the formal regularity of the French and classical models. The conclusion places him among the great teachers of life, whose faults are those of an age and whose beauties are of all ages.
narrative_structure: A continuous argumentative essay in sections, the objections stated and answered, with the illustrations drawn from the plays and with the comparative examples of the ancients and of Milton.
literary_form: critical essay and dissertation on a poet
meter_and_prosody: A firm and well-tempered critical prose of the mid-century essay, with the balanced refutation and the quoted line of proof; the sentences are periodic and the argument explicit.
historical_context: Published anonymously in 1769, in the season of the revived Shakespeare editions and of the debate about his regularity kindled by the previous generation's critics, and within the society of the Bluestockings, whose conversations had prepared the argument.
literary_significance: It gave the apologetic tradition of Shakespeare its most composed statement by a woman critic and helped to fix the moral, rather than formal, justification of his supremacy in later taste.
attribution_notes: Attribution is established rather than asserted on the title-page: the essay was published anonymously in 1769 and has been assigned to the writer on the grounds of her own papers, her circle's testimony and the later acknowledgement; authorship is therefore recorded as single with this explanation.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1769 in a small octavo, with several issues and reprints in the same year and in the following decade; the attribution is discussed in the standard editions of her letters.

title: To the Ladies
description: A short ironic poem addressed to women, remonstrating against the conditions of marriage and against the education that makes a wife a dependent. It is one of the most anthologised lyrics of the debate about women, and its couplets turn the commonplaces of gallantry against the law and custom that they conceal.
plot_or_argument: The poet addresses her sex with a complaint of their treatment, showing that they are educated only to please and are then governed by the men they have pleased. Marriage is represented as a condition in which the wife's person and estate pass into another's keeping, and the language of superiority used against women is turned back upon it. The poem closes on the advice that the ladies improve their minds and their use of them.
narrative_structure: A single continuous address in closed couplets, moving from complaint to argument to counsel; there is no narrative, the argument being carried by the sequence of the retorts.
literary_form: ironic address in verse; poem of the women question
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of the plain Augustan manner, the point of the argument closing on the rhyme; the idiom is that of the conversation poem of the debate about the sexes.
historical_context: Written in the circles of learned women of the south-west in the last years of the seventeenth century, circulating in manuscript, and appearing in print among her poems in 1703, in the season of the pamphlet and stage war about women's abilities that produced the essays and the verse poems of the question.
literary_significance: It is a landmark of early feminist verse and one of the most quoted of the period's poems on marriage and women's condition, much used in the modern recovery of the writing of women before the eighteenth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution to the poet is settled by the manuscript tradition and by the printed collections that carry her name; the poem existed in more than one state, so the year recorded here is that of the printed collection and not of composition.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1703 among the poems of its author's collected verse of that year, the text having circulated previously in manuscript; the composition date is left undetermined because the manuscript copies cannot be ordered, and the year given is that of the printed collection.

title: An Essay to Defend the Women's Cause
alternative_titles: An Essay to Defend the Womens Cause
Essay to Defend the Women's Cause
description: A prose defence of women's rational capacity and of their title to education, written in answer to the libels of the stage and of the pamphlets and arguing the equality of souls and of understanding. It circulated in manuscript before its printing and stands among the earliest English essays in the systematic defence of the sex.
plot_or_argument: The essay examines the usage by which women are reproached as fools and as unfit for learning, and denies the charge by the evidence of the understanding and of virtue. It argues that the defects charged on women are the effects of their education and of their law, not of their nature, and that the same capacity appears where the same advantages have been given. It closes with the claim that the defence of the sex is a cause of reason and of religion.
narrative_structure: A continuous argumentative essay, the objection stated, the particulars answered one by one, and the general conclusion drawn on the capacity and the deserts of women.
literary_form: polemical and argumentative essay in prose
meter_and_prosody: A direct and closely reasoned prose of the plain style, with the quick retort and the summed antithesis; the argumentative paragraphs close on a balanced sentence.
historical_context: Written in the aftermath of the stage reform quarrel and of the pamphlet war on the women question, and circulated among the learned women of the western circles before being printed at the beginning of the eighteenth century.
literary_significance: It is a founding text of the English argument for women's rational equality, standing between the defence tradition of the previous century and the educational proposals of the following one.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the essay circulated in manuscript under the author's name and was printed at the beginning of the eighteenth century, the date of the first printing being given here as conventionally assigned.
bibliographical_notes: Circulated in manuscript copies of the period and first printed in 1701 in a short tract; it is now read from the modern scholarly edition of the poet's works, which collates the manuscript versions.

title: Friendship in Death
alternative_titles: Friendship in Death: In Twenty-Six Letters, Between Two Persons of Distinction, Of the Other World
description: A series of letters between two departed friends who write to each other from their tombs in Westminster Abbey, reviewing the lives they have left and the affections they have not lost. It is one of the most original of the pious fictions of the early century, and a landmark both of the women's friendship tradition and of the literature of the other world.
plot_or_argument: Two women long deceased carry on a correspondence from their respective sepulchres, each reporting the state of the other's family and the changes of the world below. They review their own past conduct, the trials of marriage, the uses of study and the comfort of religion, and they intercede and sympathise with one another across the boundary of death. The letters pass to the deaths of those still living and to the reunions of the friends, the whole closing on the hope of a friendship perfected in another state.
narrative_structure: A serial epistolary fiction of short letters, the sequence of correspondents and of posthumous reports supplying the order; the inset histories of the living make it a collection of tales within a correspondence.
principal_characters: the two departed friends who write from their tombs; the surviving families and friends reported to them; the several characters of the inset histories
literary_form: epistolary fiction and pious romance
meter_and_prosody: A warm and elevated epistolary prose of the female devotional style, with the apostrophes to the dead and to the Abbey as its characteristic movement; some of the pieces are versified.
historical_context: Published in 1728 by a poet already known as the author of pious verse and of the poems of the earlier years, in the season of the vogue for the letters of the dead and for the conversation of the other world, an amusement that had been licensed by the essays of the previous generation.
literary_significance: It stands between the conduct fiction and the novel of female friendship, and its device of the correspondence of the dead anticipates both the Gothic letter and the sentimental fiction of bereavement; it was long read and reprinted through the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the posthumous collections of her works.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1728 in duodecimo with the letters on other subjects appended, and reissued frequently in the following decades and in the collected works of the middle of the century.

title: The History of Joseph
alternative_titles: The History of Joseph: A Poem
description: A narrative poem on the patriarch Joseph, retelling the scriptural history of the dreamer, the sold slave, the tempted servant in Potiphar's house and the exalted minister of Egypt. It is the largest of the author's verse undertakings and one of the most read of the century's scriptural poems.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the Genesis narrative from the dreams of the boy and the envy of his brethren to their journey into Egypt and the discovery of their guilt. It dwells on the temptation by Potiphar's wife and on Joseph's refusal, on the prison and the interpretation of dreams, and on the final discovery of Joseph to his family. The argument is at once providential and moral, the purity and patience of the hero being held up as an example of the government of the passions.
narrative_structure: A continuous narrative poem in books and divisions following the scriptural sequence, with the lyrical addresses and the moral reflections interposed at the crises of the story.
principal_characters: Joseph; his father and his brethren; Potiphar and his wife; the butler and the baker of the prison; Pharaoh
literary_form: scriptural narrative poem
meter_and_prosody: Narrative verse of the moderate middle style, in the blank verse and the strophic lyric measures proper to the paraphrase tradition of the day, the pathetical scenes being carried in the slower line.
historical_context: Published in 1736 by a poet long established as the century's most admired writer of pious verse, in the season of the vogue for the scriptural paraphrase and for the sacred poem as a female preserve.
literary_significance: It is a central example of the sacred narrative poem by a woman in the eighteenth century and much of the century's taste for the chaste and pathetic scripture story is formed by it and by its imitators.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the collections of her works after her death.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in London in 1736 in a handsomely issued volume in octavo or quarto with the engraving, and reissued in the posthumous collections of her prose and verse.

title: The Turkish Embassy Letters
alternative_titles: Letters Written During the Turkish Embassy
description: The correspondence of the ambassador's wife at Constantinople and Adrianople, describing the seraglios, the baths, the Greek church and the women's society of the Turkish capital, and reporting the inoculation practice she afterwards brought to England. It is the most vivacious of the century's travel writing and the classic account of the East seen by a woman.
plot_or_argument: The letters follow the party from Vienna through the Hungarian and Bulgarian roads to Adrianople and Constantinople, giving an account of the way of travelling, of the houses and of the ceremonies of the embassy. They describe the women's baths and the seraglio, the Greek ladies and their usages, and the cathedral of the Phanar, with the writer's own freedom of access to a society closed to other travellers. The later letters from the embassy report the smallpox operation, and the correspondence closes with the return into Poland and Germany.
narrative_structure: A continuous family correspondence, chiefly to a single friend, ordered by the route and the stay, and rising to the set descriptions of the baths and the seraglio; there is no plot beyond the journey and the observation.
principal_characters: the writing lady of the embassy; the friend at home to whom the letters are addressed; the begum or lady of the seraglio and her attendants; the Greek ladies of Constantinople; the ambassador and his household
literary_form: travel letters and familiar correspondence
meter_and_prosody: An animated epistolary prose of the quick phrase, the parenthesis and the indignant comparison, its sentences built on the sudden turn of observation rather than on the balanced period.
historical_context: Written during the embassy of 1717-18 at the time of the Turkish war and the settlement of the Passarowitz season, in the current of the correspondence of the diplomatic corps, and returned to by the writer's own account of inoculation in the English medical press.
literary_significance: It created the literary image of the Turkish women's world for English readers and is a foundational text of the travel letter and of the female account of the East, its evidence on inoculation being of the history of medicine as well as of letters.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the letters remained in manuscript and were given to the press after the writer's death, so that no publication year in her lifetime can be asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Written 1717-18, partly pirated into print in the years after her death and first published in a collected form from the family papers at the beginning of the nineteenth century; the record therefore carries composition dates only.

title: Solomon on the Vanity of the World
description: A reflective poem on the Preacher's theme, in which the riches, pleasures and honours of the world are weighed against the wisdom that knows their end. It is the most ambitious of its author's serious pieces and the one by which his contemporaries judged him a philosopher as well as a wit.
plot_or_argument: The poet follows the Solomon of Ecclesiastes through the trial of magnificence, building, planting and possessing, and finds the account of all his labour to be vanity. The poem passes over the conditions of the wise man and the fool, the fortune of the wicked and the rewards of the just, and resolves the enquiry into the fear of God and the government of the present heart. The close turns from the world measured to the world renounced.
narrative_structure: A sustained meditative poem in the manner of the ode and the essay in verse, the argument advancing by the review of the several species of worldly good and their judgment.
literary_form: meditative and didactic poem
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic meditative verse of the ode manner, with a regular rhyme scheme and balanced antithetical lines carrying the moral argument in the Dryden school.
historical_context: Written in the later years of a career divided between diplomacy and poetry, when the poet had been disappointed of employment and had turned to the serious essay in verse; it belongs to the company of the century's vanity-of-the-world poems.
literary_significance: It shows the other face of the most popular light poet between the two greatest of the age, and its manner of argumentative couplet meditation was a school for the younger writers who at once imitated and dismissed him.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem exists in more than one state and length, and the several issues are dated variously in the catalogues of the trade, so the year given is that of the earliest collected printing and no year of composition is asserted.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1718 among the poet's serious verse and reprinted in the collected editions of his works; the year given is that of the usual accounting of the poem, and no year of composition is asserted because the piece is assigned by modern editors to the years of his political disappointment rather than to a single date.

title: Poems on Several Occasions (Prior)
description: The collected poems of the diplomatist and wit, gathering the tales, the songs, the epistles, the translations and the grave meditations that made him the most imitated familiar verse-writer between the two greater poets who admired and censured him. The collection settled his reputation and his place in the school of English light verse.
plot_or_argument: The volume brings together the narrative tales in the manner of the old romance and of the fabliau, the songs and catch-poems of the club, the familiar epistles to friends and patrons, the paraphrases from the psalms and the translations of the ancients and of the moderns. Its compass runs from the professed gallantry of the love-poems to the moral gravity of the meditative pieces. The arrangement is that of the author's career rather than of a design.
narrative_structure: A collected miscellaneous volume ordered by species - tales, songs, epistles, translations and serious verse - with no overarching plot or argument beyond the range of the manner.
principal_characters: the several persons of the tales and epistles; the friends and patrons of the dedications; the lovers and the companions of the songs
literary_form: collected miscellany of poems
meter_and_prosody: The full range of the easy Augustan manner: the flowing couplet of the tale and epistle, the lyric measures of the songs, and the longer stanzas of the meditative poems, all marked by an affectation of negligence that is the poet's most studied art.
historical_context: Gathered in the years of the poet's employment and disappointment, in the season of the miscellany and of the collected volume as the instrument of a literary reputation, and before the long dispute between his friends and the next generation of versifiers.
literary_significance: It fixed the familiar and narrative style that the following generation learned from it, and the collection's tales and songs are a principal source of the century's idea of the easy verse between Dryden and Pope.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the collected volume carries the author's name, and the several pieces have a separate history in the pamphlets and miscellanies of the preceding years.
bibliographical_notes: The first collected issue of the poems belongs to the opening years of the century's second decade, further volumes and revised collections following in the author's later years and after his death; the year here given for the collected edition follows the project's author record, and the several issues are not separately dated.

title: The Careless Husband
description: A comedy brought out by the Drury Lane company at the end of 1704 and printed in the following year, which keeps the machinery of Restoration sexual intrigue but redirects it towards the reformation of a rake and the reconciliation of a married couple. Its central conceit, a woman's virtue tested while she lies unsuspecting and asleep, supplied the eighteenth century's most celebrated showcase for an actress. The play is habitually cited as the hinge between the libertine comedy of the 1690s and the sentimental domestic drama of the following generations.
plot_or_argument: Sir Charles Easy, a hot-tempered and inattentive husband, has come to believe that his wife Lady Easy has countenanced the addresses of Lord Careless, a gay seducer whose boast is that no woman has yet refused him. The jealousy of the husband and the vanity of the rake are answered by a stratagem of the wife's own: she writes the assignation, then contrives that she shall be found asleep in a posture that seems to invite surprise. Lord Careless, admitted to the chamber and discovering the unconscious lady, contends with himself, leaves the written appointment unfilled, and abandons the design. In the underplot the young fop Sir Easy Foppington, lately and unwillingly married, makes a fool of himself in courtship of the housemaid, and the valet Moody is detected in picking his master's pocket. Convinced by these proofs of his wife's constancy, Sir Charles asks her pardon; the reformed rake is reconciled to the family he had traduced, and the comedy closes with forgiveness and marriages.
narrative_structure: Five-act stage comedy with a main plot and a fop underplot tightly linked by their shared subject of tried virtue; the movement runs from suspicion through a single staged trial of a woman's constancy to public vindication and marriage, with the sleeping scene at the centre as the turning-point.
principal_characters: Sir Charles Easy; Lady Easy; Lord Careless; Sir Easy Foppington; Moody the valet; the chambermaid courted by the young fop
literary_form: Domestic comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, written for a particular acting company and printed from the theatre's text.
meter_and_prosody: Familiar prose speech with quick re-partee and deliberate pauses, the pauses carrying the moral weight of the sleeping scene; the customary prologue and epilogue spoken to the audience are in closed couplets.
historical_context: The manager-actor who wrote it had helped to run the Drury Lane company since the patent lapsed in 1695, and the piece answers the stage-anti-stage campaign of the 1690s by offering a comedy in which seduction is refused and reform is won on the stage. The fop plot continues the city-marriage and chambermaid intrigue that the same management had made its stock in trade. The play held the repertory through the century and remained a trial of skill for leading performers.
literary_significance: It is the standard example of the century's turn from libertine wit to sentimental proof of female constancy, and it gave the stage a situation, a woman's virtue tested in her own unconsciousness, that novelists of the next generation and later domestic drama exploited. Its mixed inheritance of intrigue and moral seriousness makes it a fixed reference point in accounts of how English comedy changed after 1700.
bibliographical_notes: First acted at the theatre royal in Drury Lane in the winter season of 1704 and printed in quarto in 1705; the text was reset for revival, was included in collections of its author's dramatic works, and was reprinted throughout the century in anthologies of English stage comedy.

title: The Non-Juror
description: An anti-Jacobite comedy brought out at Drury Lane in the winter of 1717 and printed with a title page dated 1718, which makes a non-juring clergyman the type of political and religious cant. Passive obedience, the oaths, and the converts of the church are laughed out of doors, and a plain British sea-officer is set against the scheming divine as the voice of national good sense. The play is also remembered for a scene that quoted the national dramatist back at itself, a passage its author withdrew when it was thought to do irreverence to the dead poet.
plot_or_argument: Doctor Wolf, a non-juring clergyman, combines disaffection to the settled succession with greed: he designs upon the fortune of a young Protestant heiress, whom he hopes to win both to his own communion and to his suit, and keeps his son in constraint and in debt. Young Wolf, a rake of the town, runs a course of his own, and the plain-spoken British officer who loves the heiress opposes the divine's arts with open national loyalty. The household dependants, whose interests Wolf professes to serve, are the instruments by which his contrivances are carried on and at last discovered; a disputed obligation pressed with a canting plea of mercy exposes the hypocrisy of the claimant. The father's principles are disavowed by the son, the heiress keeps her fortune and her party, and the comedy ends in the exposure of the divine rather than in a reconciliation.
narrative_structure: Five acts of prose comedy organised as a double opposition, the designing hypocrite in the house and the plain British officer against him; the plotting moves through forged claims and overheard counsel to a public unmasking in the final act.
principal_characters: Doctor Wolf, the non-juring clergyman; Young Wolf, his son; the bluff British sea-officer; the rich Protestant heiress whose fortune is designed upon; the dependants of Wolf's household
literary_form: Political comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, written for the patent theatre and printed close to performance.
meter_and_prosody: Plain prose dialogue with set speeches of some formality for the party argument; the addresses to the audience are in closed couplets, and the quotation that gave offence is taken from the blank verse of the national stage.
historical_context: It was written in the temper of the years after the rising of 1715, when non-juring churchmen were a visible and legally precarious class, and it belongs to the flush of anti-Jacobite stage writing that followed the settlement of the succession. The divine supposed to be satirised complained of a libel and proceeded against the publisher, but the complaint did not prosper. The management that staged it had by then made party business of loyalty on the stage.
literary_significance: It is the most direct instance of a patent-house comedy written as party warfare, and the one play of its era that made the non-juring clergyman a stock stage character. The history of its suppressed Shakespearean scene is a document in the rising reverence for the bard, and its use of hypocrisy for party ends measures how far the comic treatment of cant had moved since the 1690s.
bibliographical_notes: First acted at Drury Lane in the winter of 1717; the earliest quarto bears the date 1718, the difference arising from the change of the new year in the old-style calendar, and the scene afterwards withdrawn by its author is present in the first issues and absent from later reprints.

title: Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber
description: An autobiographical memoir published in 1740 after the writer's retirement from the stage, at once a defence of a career and the richest contemporary account of the London patent theatre in its first brilliant half-century. Written in a garrulous, self-admiring prose that rarely distinguishes vanity from evidence, it reviews the author's own plays and acting, the quarrels and collapses of the companies he helped to manage, and the attacks of his enemies, the most formidable of which had long since enthroned him as the emperor of dullness.
plot_or_argument: The narrative runs from a boyhood in the theatre world and a first sight of a play to management at Drury Lane, feuds with rival companies and with the poets who succeeded, and final retirement; it is interrupted by set defences of the author's treatment of the Shakespearean text, of his own dramatic writings, and of the actors and actresses he employed. Passages of portraiture of players, managers and their noble patrons are worked up from memory and were repeatedly borrowed by later historians of the stage. The memoir prints or paraphrases the prologues, epilogues and occasional verses by which its author had advertised himself, and quotes the insults levelled at him at length so as to return them with good humour.
narrative_structure: Continuous first-person prose narrative running in one line from youth to old age, with documentary matter - verses, letters, the published records of quarrels - embedded in it and with digressive chapters on the drama and on editorial dealings with the national dramatist.
principal_characters: the author himself as boy, actor, manager and old man; the players and actresses of the two patent houses; the booksellers and rivals with whom he quarrelled; the noble patrons and box-keepers of the theatre
literary_form: Autobiographical memoir and theatrical history in prose.
historical_context: The memoir was put together in the years of the author's retirement, when the theatre he described had been reconstituted by new managers and licences, and when the satire that had made his name a byword for dullness was still in circulation. It belongs to the flourishing of theatrical memoir and anecdote that also produced the biographical prefaces of the play collections of the 1730s and 1740s, and it is a specimen of the Augustan practice of answering lampoon with autobiography.
literary_significance: It is the principal source-book for the company history, repertory and acting style of the London stage between the 1680s and the 1730s, and the standard illustration of how a manager turned autobiography into reply. Historians use its testimony with caution because self-love governs its dates and its judgments, and its apology for adapting the national dramatist to modern taste is the fullest contemporary defence of that practice.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1740 and frequently reprinted; modern scholarly editions, with commentary on its theatrical and political allusions, correct its chronology and are the basis for the dates used in this record. The year of composition is left undetermined because the memoir was written over a long period of retirement and cannot be assigned to a single date.

title: The Confederacy
description: A city comedy brought out and printed in 1705 which replaces the wits and rakes of the 1690s with two rich, jealous money-scriveners and their confederating wives. The plot is built out of surveillance and counter-plotting: the husbands watch each other and their wives, and the women combine to turn that jealousy against its authors. Long judged the best of its author's later comedies, it depends for its effect on the pressure of two mirrored households set side by side.
plot_or_argument: Gripe and Money-trap, two wealthy City husbands of suspicious and niggardly temper, are each persuaded that the other's wife has designs upon his own affections; Clarissa distrusts Araminta and Money-trap watches Clarissa. Against this surveillance the two wives form the confederacy of the title, with the help of the gossips Mrs. Amlet and Mrs. Cloggit, and lay a scheme in which Dick, a young gamester, serves as the apparent instrument. Their design is to draw the jealous husbands into the outlay and the loss of a considerable sum, and to make their watchfulness the means of their own deception, while the serving-men Brass and Clip carry the messages that keep the two houses in ignorance of each other. The discovery at the last leaves the husbands defrauded of their suspicions together with their money, the wives in quiet possession of the field, and the gamester provided for. The interest of the play is not moral reformation but the mechanics of a trick well done.
narrative_structure: Five acts of prose comedy in which the two households alternate scene by scene; the action is carried by concealed letters, eavesdropping and mistaken jealousy, and resolves by discovery rather than by penitence.
principal_characters: Gripe; Money-trap; Clarissa; Araminta; Dick the gamester; Brass; Clip; Mrs. Amlet; Mrs. Cloggit; Corinna
literary_form: City comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, spoken from the theatre's own text.
meter_and_prosody: Brisk prose dialogue with short alternating speeches and soliloquies of suspicion; the addresses to the audience are in closed couplets.
historical_context: It was acted and printed in the year following the settlement of the patent theatres into their Drury Lane and Lincoln's Inn Fields rivalries, and its money-scriveners belong to the long stage tradition of the jealous citizen which the comedy of the 1670s and 1690s had exploited. Its author, a gentleman dramatist and officer of arms, wrote here for the City audience of the patent house, and the play's treatment of wedlock, covetousness and female alliance carries the debate about the immorality of the stage into the counting-house.
literary_significance: It is the strongest surviving example of its author's mature comic method and one of the last plays in which the City-household plot of the Restoration stage is rebuilt entirely in terms of female alliance. The confederate wives and the use of jealousy as a mere engine of plot look forward to the domestic intrigue of the following century, and its construction has often been preferred to that of comedies now better known.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1705 in quarto, the edition professedly taken from the manager's book of the theatre royal in Drury Lane, which is the firmest external evidence of the house at which it was played; it has since been reprinted in the collected dramatic works, where it stands by itself apart from the companion comedy of the same season.

title: The Provok'd Husband
description: The comedy which its first author left unfinished at his death in 1726, worked up for the stage by the Drury Lane management and acted and printed in 1728. It returns to the provoked-wife material of the 1690s and turns it into a reform comedy of marriage, in which a gadabout and gamester wife is brought back to her duties by an artifice practised on the whole household. As an acting text it belongs to the sentimental reconstitution of London comedy in the 1720s.
plot_or_argument: Lord Townly, a husband of some patience, is driven to distraction by Lady Townly, who loves play, the card-table and general company more than her house, and who is encouraged in her courses by her visiting friends and by an intriguing foreign count who designs upon the women about her. The husband's remedy is an artifice of his own: he gives out that he is dying, and lets the household, his wife included, rehearse its grief in his hearing, so that their real calculations of profit and freedom appear beneath the forms of mourning. On the pretended recovery he uses what he has overheard to rebuke and reclaim his wife, and the last acts move the circle from conspiracy to penitence. The subplots of servants and dependants, who read the master's disguise differently, supply the lower register of the same exposure.
narrative_structure: Five acts of prose comedy divided between the fashionably dissolute wife's outside courses and the domestic exposure that closes them; the feigned deathbed is the structural hinge, and the reform of the wife is effected by testimony rather than by argument.
principal_characters: Lord Townly; Lady Townly, his gamester and gadabout wife; her fashionable friends; the foreign count who designs upon them; the servants and dependants of the household
literary_form: Domestic comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, an acting text made up from an unfinished draft.
meter_and_prosody: Spoken prose throughout, with the moral set-pieces of the exposure in short formal passages and the closing address to the audience in couplets.
historical_context: The original author had died leaving the play a fragment, and the manager who produced it finished it for a January production in 1728, the season in which sentimental domestic comedy had become the profitable form of the patent house. The share taken by the finisher was afterwards enlarged in his own memoirs and disputed by the friends of the deceased writer, and the two hands were never cleanly separated. The piece entered the century's repertory and was revived repeatedly.
literary_significance: It kept the provoked-wife argument of the 1690s alive as a reform comedy and supplied the stage with a durable scene of pretended death and detected grief. As a text it is the standard illustration of collaborative canon formation in the eighteenth-century theatre, and the two surviving states of one comedy make it a case study in posthumous revision.
attribution_notes: Finished and adapted for the stage by the Drury Lane manager who produced it; the printed text names the deceased author alone, the extent of the completion was contested at once, and the play is therefore entered here as collaborative with the first share being the unfinished draft.
bibliographical_notes: First acted at Drury Lane in January 1728 and printed in the same year; modern collected editions print the unfinished design under the title by which its author had announced it alongside the completed acting text, so that the two states of the comedy can be compared. No separate year of composition is assigned because the draft belongs to the last years of the first author's life and the acting text to 1728.

title: The Judgment of Paris
description: A masque written in 1701 for the musical prize contested by the chief composers of the day, and not seen as a stage entertainment until the Haymarket production of 1712. The classical fable of the apple and the three goddesses is recast as an English pastoral contest, in which the rival claims of power, wisdom and beauty are set out for music rather than for dramatic action. The piece is the only considerable dramatic writing of its author's mature years, and it reads as a study in how a poet may build a text to be set.
plot_or_argument: Celestial machinery opens the fable anew, and the three goddesses descend to the shepherd Paris on Ida that he may judge their appeals as of old. Juno offers power and extended empire, Pallas offers wisdom and renown in arms, and Venus offers beauty and the pleasures of love; each claim is urged in set airs and in recitative addressed to the shepherd's judgment. Paris, who is already beloved by the nymph Oenone, awards the prize to Venus, and the desert of the forsaken nymph supplies the tender undercurrent that keeps the allegory from being merely a programme. The several appeals are commented upon by pastoral attendants and by choruses, so that the moral of the choice is delivered in the alternation of musical effects rather than by argument, and the closing matter commends the triumph of beauty to the audience of the day.
narrative_structure: A masque in three acts for singers, machinery and chorus; the dramatic line is subordinated to a sequence of competitive appeals and their musical answers, with an opening invocation and a celebratory close.
principal_characters: Jupiter; Juno; Pallas; Venus; Paris the shepherd; Oenone the forsaken nymph; the attendants of the goddesses and the pastoral chorus
literary_form: Masque or libretto for sung drama in three acts, composed as a competition text for the music prize of 1701.
meter_and_prosody: Deliberately varied lyric line-lengths, short song-measures set off against longer declamatory lines for recitative, a prosody designed to give the composer distinct musical occasions; the choral and closing matter is in brisk regular rhyme.
historical_context: The libretto was written for the musical contest of the spring and summer of 1701, in which several composers set the same English poem, an episode in the attempt to sustain an English musical drama after the generation of the great court composers. The interval of eleven years between the prize and the full stage production at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket in March 1712 measures the small market for such work before the Italian vogue of the following decade changed conditions. The poet had by then abandoned the public stage for other employments, and this text stands alone among his later writings for the theatre.
literary_significance: It preserves the only masque written by the foremost comedy-writer of his generation and is a document of the English effort to make serious musical drama out of an allegorical fable. Its graded lyric lines, adjusted to the composer's convenience, were long cited as a model of the poet's service to music, and the piece marks the late reach of the masque tradition into the competitive concert and opera life of London.
bibliographical_notes: The text was printed in London in 1701 in connection with the music prize, the several competing settings being the evidence for the order of that trial; the first entire stage performance was at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket in March 1712, and the masque was afterwards reprinted among the author's poetical and lyrical works.

title: The Commonwealth of Slaves
description: The second part of the stage adaptation of the Oroonoko story, brought out for the Drury Lane stage at the turn of the century and printed in 1701. Where the first part had made the African prince's constancy and betrayal the substance of a tearful tragedy, the continuation carries the consequence into rebellion, siege and execution, and keeps the comedy of planter appetite running beneath it. The very title, a commonwealth of slaves, makes the plantation a scene of political danger as well as of pity.
plot_or_argument: Oroonoko, sold into the plantations and still honoured as a prince by those about him, finds that the colony's laws leave him no redress, and combines the captives into an armed community resolved to win its liberty or to die. Imoinda, who has followed him into bondage and bears him a child in the new world, is the occasion both of his tenderness and of his exposure. The English planters conduct the suppression with a cruelty that the play invites its audience to measure against their Christian profession: the widow of fortune who had pursued the slave with her purse, the governor and the trading captain who first cozened him, and the young heiress whose suit is disputed among them, all pursue their several bargains while the revolt is being crushed. The rising is betrayed and put down, Oroonoko is taken, scourged and destroyed, and the subordinate plots close in marriage or in the discomfiture of the greedy. The tragedy is thus carried from the pathos of betrayal to the politics of a slave republic and its suppression.
narrative_structure: Tragedy in five acts with a two-tier design, the heroic line in verse and the plantation underplot in prose; the first part's single movement of betrayal is here expanded into plotting, discovery and military suppression.
principal_characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; the widow of fortune who designs upon the hero; the governor of the colony; the captain who betrayed him; the planter family about whom the underplot turns; the followers of the slave community
literary_form: Heroic tragedy in five acts, the continuation of an adaptation already recorded, written for the patent house and printed from the acting text.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic five-beat line for the heroic roles, with couplets closing the scenes of the prince's speeches; the planter underplot is in prose, with the song matter of the earlier part reduced.
historical_context: The adaptation had held the London stage since the middle of the 1690s and was the most frequently revived treatment on the English theatre of African slavery and of African nobility. The continuation appeared in the years when the royal trade in captives was a matter of charter and of parliamentary dispute, and when the plantations were becoming a visible political question.
