Its title plays upon the vocabulary of rebellion and of contested government which the previous century had made familiar to every playhouse audience.
literary_significance: It completes the most influential stage version of the tale and, by converting the first part's pathos into a slave revolt and its suppression, brought the politics of plantation slavery into the tragedy of the patent theatre. Its two-tier handling of African heroism and English avarice became the standard framework for later treatments of the subject, and it remains a fixed reference in the history of the stage Oroonoko.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1701 as the second part of the adaptation and described on the title page as acted at the Theatre Royal in Drury Lane; the surviving theatrical papers of the season do not fix the first day of performance, and that date is therefore left undetermined here. Modern editions usually print this continuation with the first part, from which it is separated in the early quartos.

title: The Christian Religion, as Professed by a Daughter of the Church of God
description: The longest and most systematic of her prose works, published in 1705 and reprinted through the century, a practical divinity written in the manner of a moral essay. It argues that Christianity is a reasonable and orderly scheme of duty, and then lays out the devotional, moral and social conduct proper to a churchwoman, with sustained sections on the government of the passions and on the duties of the single and the married state. The title announces the standpoint: an account of religion written from within the communion, and addressed to practice rather than to controversy.
plot_or_argument: The first division establishes the grounds of belief, the evidence of revelation and the authority of the church, and answers the pretences of free enquiry and of latitudinarian moderation which would relax those grounds for the sake of ease or of party. The second division reduces the Christian life to a method: a settled rule of devotion, periodical self-examination, the ordering of the affections towards the love of God, and the practice of charity and of the duties of each station. Along the way she argues that the Passions, esteem, and the love of the world are the real enemies of a devout life, and that the conscience must be disciplined by the church's rule instead of left to its own temper. The whole is intended as a complete guide to conduct for a reader who means to think and to believe consistently.
narrative_structure: Treatise in two main divisions, speculative grounds followed by a rule of life in numbered practical sections; the manner is sententious and hortatory, with long periodic sentences and frequent appeal to the reader's own experience.
literary_form: Practical divinity and conduct treatise in prose, a devotional and moral system rather than an occasional controversy.
historical_context: It appeared in 1705, after the occasional conformity controversies of the last years of the war had sharpened the language of church party, and between her earlier philosophical writings and the high-church polemic of the following decade. Its assertion that Christianity is a reasonable service answers the latitudinarian and deist vocabularies then current, and its tone is that of a woman writing within the communion's discipline for readers of both sexes. The bookseller who issued it had printed her occasional prose, and it passed through many editions without the name of its author on the title page.
literary_significance: It is her most ambitious prose work and the one by which she was best known to readers who never reached her scheme of female education. Its blending of conduct book, practical divinity and moral philosophy is the fullest evidence of the religious content of her case for women, and the number of its editions measures the reach of a woman's prose theology in the early eighteenth century.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1705 in a single volume and reprinted repeatedly in the following decades, sometimes with altered title-page dating; the year of composition cannot be determined and is left blank here. It is best consulted in the modern scholarly reprint, whose commentary on its sources has settled the chronology of her prose used in this record.

title: Parables, in Two Parts
description: Two allegorical prose fictions published together in 1705, in which the distempers of church and nation are represented under the veil of a vision. The borrowed form, a conference of personified claims reported by an observer, lets its writer say in parable what a sermon or an occasional tract could less well maintain. The style is ornate, rhythmic and charged with scriptural cadence, and the argument is as much devotional as political.
plot_or_argument: The reader is admitted to a sequence of personified conferences in which the complaints of the age are tried as in a vision: the claims of conscience against the claims of authority, the flatteries of the world against the discipline of a rule of life, and the divisions of a nation against the unity it is called to maintain. The argument running through both parts is that a people which relaxes its religion in order to compound with its politics will lose both, and that the private Christian's remedy is a settled conduct founded on the teaching of the church. The allegory is transparent enough to be read as church and party commentary and plain enough to serve as devotional counsel. The observer reports, applies and exhorts, and the two parts close in the same remonstrance with the conscience of the age.
narrative_structure: Two parables in two parts, each a framed vision or conference with personified speakers, with the application attached to the figure; the sequence is argumentative rather than narrative.
principal_characters: the observing narrator; the personified claims of conscience, of authority and of the world
literary_form: Allegorical prose fiction; a pair of devotional and political parables in the visionary conference manner.
historical_context: It was printed in 1705, the year after the occasional conformity measure had divided the parties and while the long war still governed the nation's politics and its church politics together. High-church writers of the period were trying allegorical and visionary forms for the language of the church in danger, and this pair of tracts belongs to that experiment rather than to the systematic prose of its author's earlier books. Its publication by the same bookseller as her other tracts kept it inside the circle of her occasional readers.
literary_significance: The parables show the range of her prose from the systematic treatise to visionary allegory, and are the best evidence of how a woman of letters used the fable form for church and party argument after the censorial assumptions of the 1690s had broken down. Their ornate rhythmic sentence is a marked instance of the scriptural manner in women's prose before the century's sermon style settled.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in two parts in London in 1705 for the bookseller who issued her other tracts, each part in a separate quarto sheet as was the custom with such publications; modern readers use the collected editions of her prose, which regularise the numbering and the spelling of the two issues.
